It’s the younger generation that doesn’t appreciate good quality these days. Everything’s disposable. Speaker_1: Mum, they're not antiques. And look, remember Hannah from university? As long as they appreciate it. It’s a shame, really. I spent years collecting these. Speaker_4: Speaking of appreciating things... did you ever finish that crossword, Margaret? I was looking at it earlier, seemed a bit tricky. Speaker_3: Not yet, John. It’s got some devilish clues. “A nocturnal bird with a thirst for knowledge.” What on earth could that be? Speaker_2: An owl? Because owls are wise... it's a bit of a cliché, though. Speaker_5: (After a long pause) Used to have an owl. In a picture. Beautiful thing. Speaker_1: (Changing the subject) Actually, about Hannah, I was thinking… maybe we could have her over for dinner next weekend? It would be lovely to see her after all this time. Speaker_2: That’s a great idea! She’s always been really good with your Auntie Carol. Speaker_3: Carol would love that! She's been asking about her constantly. We'll have to make a proper fuss then. Roast chicken, I think. Speaker_4: (Nodding) Roast chicken sounds lovely. And some carrots. Proper, old-fashioned roast chicken and carrots. Just like it used to be. Speaker_5: (Quietly) Carrots… good with a bit of butter. Speaker_1: (Smiling warmly, looking around at everyone) Yeah, good with a bit of butter.

Speaker_1: (Stirring her food thoughtfully) This shepherd's pie is lovely, isn't it? You’ve really outdone yourself tonight, love. Speaker_2: (Chewing enthusiastically) Mmm-hmm! Best ever! Can I have more peas, please? Speaker_1: (Smiling) Of course, sweetheart. More peas coming right up. Right, so, about work. It was a bit… chaotic today. You won't believe what happened with the Henderson account. Speaker_2: Henderson? Is that the grumpy one? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) You've met him, haven’t you? Yes, the grumpy one. Apparently, he’s decided he doesn't like the new brochure design. After we've been working on it for six weeks! The feedback was ridiculously vague, too – just, “It doesn't *feel* right.” Honestly, I nearly pulled my hair out. Speaker_2: That's not fair! You work so hard. Did you tell him how you felt? Speaker_1: (Sighs) I tried to be diplomatic, darling. Explained the design choices, the research… but he just kept saying it wasn't capturing his brand essence. Marketing meetings can be so draining sometimes. I’m just glad it’s Friday. Skiing tomorrow! Speaker_2: Skiing! Yippee! Are we going to see snow? Speaker_1: (Ruffling her hair) I really, really hope so! The forecast looks promising, lots of fluffy white stuff predicted. And you’ve got your new snow boots, haven’t you? We need to make sure those are zipped up tight! Last time you fell over trying to build a snowman. Speaker_2: I did! But that was *because* it was icy. And Daddy helped me up! Speaker_1: (Laughing) He did, didn’t he? He's always got your back. Right, so, I was thinking, maybe we should book a ski lesson for you? Just a short one, to get you comfortable with the basics. Speaker_2: A lesson? With a teacher? I can ski! I slid down the little hill at the park! Speaker_1: (Smiling patiently) That's lovely, darling. But the slopes in the Alps are a *little* different. It's just to make sure you're safe and having fun. And I can have a proper go on the black runs while you’re having your lesson. Speaker_2: Can I have hot chocolate with marshmallows after? Speaker_1: (Leaning across the table to kiss her forehead) Absolutely. The biggest, most marshmallow-filled hot chocolate you've ever seen. So, are you excited about the holiday now? Speaker_2: (Nodding vigorously) Yes! Are we going to see mountains? Big mountains? Speaker_1: You are! Huge, snowy mountains. And we’ll build a snowman with a carrot nose, and maybe even have a snowball fight. What do you think? Speaker_2: (Clapping her hands) Snowball fight! But be careful not to hit Daddy! Speaker_1: (Smiling) I’ll try my best. Though he's a pretty good snowball thrower himself. You know, this work stuff feels a million miles away now, doesn't it? A week in the mountains with you two is exactly what I needed. Speaker_2: Can I pack my teddy? Barnaby needs a holiday too! Speaker_1: Of course, Barnaby is coming! He needs to experience the snow, doesn’t he? Now, finish your peas. We need to get you packed before tomorrow morning! And I need a lie-down after dealing with Mr. Henderson.

Speaker_1: (Sighs dramatically, flopping onto a beanbag chair) Honestly, Chloe, this Maths homework is *criminal*. Like, who decided quadratic equations were a good idea at fifteen? It’s just… meaningless. Speaker_2: (Sitting cross-legged on the floor, fiddling with her phone) Tell me about it. Mr. Davies seems to think we're all about to become rocket scientists. I swear, I spent the entire lesson drawing little doodles of pineapples instead of focusing. Are you even *starting* on it? Speaker_1: Started? I *glanced* at it. One equation. One. It spat back a cryptic error message. I’m giving up. We should be learning about music production instead. Much more useful. Speaker_2: You’re obsessed with that GarageBand thing, aren't you? It's pretty cool though. You've got a real knack for it. Did you lay down any new beats today? Speaker_1: I tried! I was going for this chilled-out, lo-fi vibe, but it just ended up sounding like a strangled cat. Still, I learned something. What about English? That essay on ‘The Great Gatsby’ due Friday feels like a mountain too. Speaker_2: Ugh, Gatsby. All that dramatic longing and expensive parties. I’m just not feeling it. Mrs. Thompson wants us to analyze symbolism, but I’m drawing a blank. What do you think the green light *really* means, anyway? Is it just… green? Speaker_1: (Chuckles) You’re terrible. It’s obviously hope and the American Dream, yeah? But like, a corrupted, unattainable version of the American Dream. It's rather sad, when you think about it. I actually got a bit into it. My mum's been reading it again, so I've been listening to her talk about it. It’s surprisingly compelling. Speaker_2: See, you're actually thinking about it! I just see millionaire problems. Anyway, less school stresses, more important things. Did you hear about the Food Tech competition? Speaker_1: The one where we have to create a dish representing our heritage? Yeah, a bit daunting, isn’t it? My mum suggested a full-on Sunday roast… it’s ambitious. Speaker_2: Ambitious is good! My gran’s got this amazing recipe for chicken and chorizo paella. I was thinking I could do that. It feels… Spanish, you know? It’s probably easier than a roast though. Less chance of setting the kitchen on fire. Speaker_1: True. Speaking of Spanish, are you sticking with your Duolingo? I’m thinking of dropping out. It’s so boring. Speaker_2: No way! I'm actually getting quite a bit better, honestly. I can order a coffee and ask for directions now. Imagine, being able to travel anywhere and actually *understand* what people are saying. Speaker_1: I guess that *would* be pretty cool. Maybe I'll give it another week. What about jobs? Dad keeps going on about us needing to think about summer jobs. Speaker_2: Seriously annoying, isn't he? I’m not sure what I’d even *do*. Babysitting? Seems boring. Although, the little ones are pretty funny sometimes. Speaker_1: I was thinking about helping out at the music shop downtown. They’re always looking for someone to sort CDs and stuff. It’s not glamorous, but at least it’s music-related, right? And I might learn a bit about different instruments. Speaker_2: That’s brilliant! See, you’re thinking practically! I'm just picturing myself stuck folding endless piles of towels at some holiday park. Yikes. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Don't say that! We’ll both find something decent. Let’s just focus on surviving quadratic equations and Gatsby first. Fancy a biscuit? Mum’s made those chocolate ones you like. Speaker_2: Definitely! And maybe after biscuits, we can actually look at that Spanish vocabulary list… a little

Speaker_1: (Settling back into an armchair with a sigh, adjusting a knitted shawl) Oh, that film was a bit much, wasn't it? All that shouting! Gave me a right headache, it did. Speaker_2: (Smiling slightly, scrolling through her phone) A little intense, yeah, but I thought the cinematography was stunning, honestly. The way they used the light… Did you notice the long takes in the desert scenes? Really pulled you in. Speaker_1: Long takes? Love a bit of a quick cut, I do. Too much staring at one thing for me, love. Makes me fidgety. What *was* it about, anyway? Seemed a bit… complicated. All that talk of legacy and redemption. Speaker_2: It's a generational story, really. About a father passing down his business to his son, but the son wants to do something different. There's a lot of conflict, obviously. And a bit of corruption thrown in. It's based on a true story, actually. Speaker_1: Corruption, is it? Don't need that sort of thing, thank you very much. Used to like a good Western, you know. Something with a clear good guy and a clear bad guy. John Wayne, now he was a proper hero. "Rio Bravo," that’s a film. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Grandma, you and John Wayne! I'm glad you enjoy those old classics, but the world's a bit more grey now, isn't it? Things aren't always black and white. Speaker_1: Grey’s dreary. Give me a bit of sunshine and a bit of a sing-song any day. Speaking of which, did you ever see "Singin' in the Rain?" Now *that's* a film. Gene Kelly, splashing about in puddles... delightful! Speaker_2: Of course! Everyone's seen "Singin’ in the Rain." It’s iconic. But it’s a very different kind of film than the one we just watched. That felt a lot more… real, wouldn’t you say? Grittier. Speaker_1: Real and gritty usually means depressing, dear. Though, I do enjoy a good drama now and then. Remember that one with Meryl Streep… the one about the iron lady? Speaker_2: "The Iron Lady"? Yeah, that was powerful. You know, talking about powerful women… I saw "Little Women" last year. Saoirse Ronan was just brilliant. It totally modernised the story, in a way, without losing the heart of it. Speaker_1: Ah, "Little Women." Read those books as a girl, I did. Jo was my favourite. Always wanted to be a writer, like her. Never turned out that way, of course. Ended up working at a grocer’s, I did. Perfectly respectable, mind you. Speaker_2: You always tell the best stories, Grandma. It’s amazing how you can weave a whole life into a conversation about films. Speaker_1: Well, dear, life *is* a film, isn't it? Full of ups and downs, comedies and tragedies. Though, I'd like to think mine’s had a few more comedies than tragedies. So, what are you fancying watching next? Anything a little lighter? Perhaps a nice musical? Speaker_2: (Thinking for a moment) Actually, I was thinking we could watch that documentary about David Attenborough. The new one on the coral reefs? I hear it’s incredible. Speaker_1: Coral reefs? Oh, I don’t know about that, dear. Seems a bit… scientific. Speaker_2: It’s beautiful! And it’s important. We need to know about these things. Besides, David Attenborough can make anything interesting. Speaker_1: (Grudgingly) Alright, alright. But if there’s too many clever words, I’m switching it off. And someone put the kettle on, will you? Watching a film is thirsty work. Especially when it's all long takes and shouting!

Speaker_1: (Sipping her coffee, looking out the window) Honestly, Mum, this rain is relentless. It's been grey for days! I'm starting to feel like a mushroom. Speaker_2: (Stirring sugar into her coffee) Aye, it’s a proper soaker, innit? Birmingham weather, always a bit unpredictable. Though, I remember winters as a girl, snow up to your knees! This is just… damp. Not unpleasant, mind you. At least the garden’s getting a good watering. Speaker_1: I suppose. I was thinking about taking Leo for a walk in Cannon Hill Park tomorrow, but if it's like this… He’ll hate it. He’s such a drama queen when he gets his paws wet. Speaker_2: He is a bit of a pampered prince, that Leo. But you’ve done a good job with him. He's a lovely dog. You should take him even if it's a bit drizzly, fresh air’s good for him. Or we could go to the botanical gardens? They've got that lovely glasshouse. Speaker_1: That’s a good shout, Mum! The glasshouse is always a winner. Right, I'll check the forecast properly tonight. Speaking of plans, have you had a think about Aunt Carol’s birthday next month? It’s her 70th, after all. Speaker_2: I have, love. I was thinking about booking a table at that Italian place she likes, La Dolce Vita, down on Broad Street. But it needs to be a Saturday, she’s got her bridge club on Tuesdays and Thursdays, you know how she is about that. Speaker_1: Perfect! I can look into availability. I was thinking we could get a cake from that bakery near the Jewellery Quarter - the one with the amazing salted caramel brownies? Speaker_2: Oh, you know how to butter me up! Yes, please do. Anything for Aunt Carol. She's been a bit down lately, hasn't she? Something to do with Mr. Henderson retiring from the court. Apparently, they were quite close. Speaker_1: Really? I hadn’t realised. That's a shame. It must be unsettling for her after working so closely with him for so long. It’s the same at the school, you know. Mr. Davies retired last year and it's completely changed the atmosphere. It's odd, isn't it, how much one person can impact a place. Speaker_2: It is, love. Keeps you grounded, though, doesn't it? Reminds you nothing stays the same. Being a court usher, you see it all the time. People’s lives on the line, families ripped apart… It's a heavy responsibility, you know. Not many people understand what we do, really. Just think of us as… the people in black robes standing around. Speaker_1: I know it’s far more than that, Mum. You’re the one keeping everything running smoothly, making sure everyone's treated fairly. It sounds exhausting sometimes. Are you thinking of retiring anytime soon? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Don't you start! I'm not ready to shuffle off just yet. Keeps me active, keeps my mind sharp. Besides, what else would I do? Knit slippers for everyone I know? Speaker_1: (Laughing) You'd probably win awards for slipper-knitting! Seriously though, you deserve a good rest. I’m worried about your knee, you know. You shouldn't be standing on your feet all day. Speaker_2: That’s just a bit of wear and tear, love. A bit of ibuprofen sorts it out. You worry too much. Just like when you were little and insisted I wasn't walking properly after I tripped over the cat! Speaker_1: (Smiling) I was a very concerned child. But that’s because I love you! Anyway, back to plans… have you seen that new Agatha Christie adaptation on the BBC? 'Why Didn't They Ask Evans?' I'm absolutely hooked. Speaker_2: Not yet,

Speaker_1: (Sighs contentedly, adjusting her scarf against the slight evening chill) Honestly, this air is just *amazing* after a day cooped up in that stuffy lecture hall. It’s so clean, isn’t it? I almost forgot what it felt like to breathe properly. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, falling into step beside her) You're romanticising a bit, love. It’s still air. And I think my sinuses are having a field day with the pollen. Did you manage to find those silk scarves you were after today? The ones with the little embroidered details? Speaker_1: I did! Well, *almost*. I found a gorgeous selection in that little shop near the university – the one we passed earlier. They had the colour scheme I wanted perfectly, a lovely dusty rose and jade green, but the embroidery wasn't quite right. Too…busy, somehow. I was envisioning something more delicate, you see. Speaker_2: Delicate is your middle name when it comes to scarves. You’ll be searching for ages then. Should we check that market tomorrow? I remember seeing a few stalls with hand-embroidered things. Maybe we’ll get lucky. Speaker_1: That’s a brilliant idea. Want to make a proper morning of it? We could grab some of those steamed buns from that little place near the entrance - you know, the ones filled with pork and vegetables? They’re divine. Speaker_2: Steamed buns it is! A very persuasive argument. Although, I’m still slightly traumatized by that last batch. Remember that one with the… unexpected burst of chilli? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, don’t remind me! I practically set my mouth on fire! It was worth it though, wasn't it? At least it was memorable. Speaking of memorable… how did that presentation to the department go this afternoon? You seemed a bit stressed this morning. Speaker_2: It was…okay. Prof. Li was being particularly difficult. Kept harping on about the need to “modernize” my teaching methods, as if I’m still teaching Chaucer with a blackboard and chalk. He clearly doesn't appreciate the value of a good, solid lecture. Speaker_1: (Nods sympathetically) Oh, that old chestnut. He just wants to implement another one of those online, interactive simulations no one actually uses. He’s obsessed. Did you manage to steer him away from that particular path of doom? Speaker_2: Mostly. I managed to convince him that a small focus group would be a better starting point, rather than a full-scale departmental overhaul. Basically, kicked the can down the road. It bought me some time. Speaker_1: Smart move. Procrastination is a valuable skill in academia. So, how’s the grant application coming along? Have you finished drafting the methodology section? Speaker_2: Almost. It’s the statistical analysis section that’s proving tricky. I’m starting to feel completely underwater with all the jargon. I might need to rope you in for a sanity check this weekend. You’re always better at deciphering that stuff. Speaker_1: Absolutely. Consider it done. I'm good at spotting statistical nonsense. Just don’t expect me to understand *why* it’s nonsense, just that it *is*. Oh, look! Our street! We're almost home. Speaker_2: Already? This walk was lovely. It’s good to just… talk, you know? Beyond marking essays and battling professors. Did you pick up tea? I'm desperately craving a pot of something strong. Speaker_1: Of course! Jasmine, your favourite. And I got those little ginger biscuits you like. Ready for a relaxing evening? Speaker_2: (Smiling, sliding his arm around her) Couldn’t be better. Let’s get in. It’s getting quite chilly, and I think that pollen is finally catching up with me.

Speaker_1: (Stirring a bowl vigorously) Right, okay, so let’s solidify this. Saturday’s the photoshoot, isn't it? And I’m still a little hazy on who’s doing what. Speaker_2: (Sitting at the kitchen table, engrossed in a picture book) Saturday! Pirates! Speaker_3: (Climbing onto a stool, reaching for a cookie) Can I have a cookie, Mummy? Are we having pirates for dinner? Speaker_1: (Chuckles, handing Speaker_3 a cookie) No pirates for dinner, love. But Saturday *is* photoshoot day! And yes, darling, (to Speaker_2) pirates are very exciting! We’ll learn all about them later. Now, about the photoshoot… Liam’s confirmed he’ll be handling the lighting, which is brilliant, right? And Aunt Sarah’s bringing her backdrop - the floral one you both loved. Speaker_2: The pretty one! Speaker_3: With the butterflies! Speaker_1: Exactly! So, that leaves… outfits. I’ve got your little outfits sorted, you two. Yours, (referring to Speaker_3), is the little sailor suit, and yours, (to Speaker_2) is the fairy dress – the one with the sparkle. But what about us? Should I stick with the dark blue dress, or try something else? Speaker_2: Fairy dress! Sparkly! Speaker_3: Sailor! Arrr! Speaker_1: (Laughing) You’re both very enthusiastic about your costumes. Okay, settled then! And I was thinking… Fiona wanted to meet up for coffee next week. Would Tuesday work? It would be lovely to catch up properly. I haven't seen her in ages. Speaker_2: Fiona! She has a puppy! Speaker_3: Puppy! Can we see puppy? Speaker_1: We absolutely can! We'll arrange it. Right, Tuesday... I’ll text her. While I do that, could you two tell me what you're reading? Speaker_2, you look completely absorbed. Speaker_2: (Holding up the book) It’s about a brave knight! He fights a dragon! Speaker_1: A brave knight, eh? Very impressive. And you, Speaker_3? Are you enjoying your pirate adventure? Speaker_3: (Mouth full of cookie) He finds treasure! Lots of gold! Speaker_1: Wonderful! It sounds lovely. Speaking of adventures, I was thinking afterwards, while we’re out for the photoshoot, we could pop into that little bookstore in Grantchester. They have a fantastic children's section. Maybe we can find a new adventure for you both. Speaker_2: Bookshop! Yes! Speaker_3: New book! Gold! Speaker_1: (Smiling) We’ll see! It depends on how long the photoshoot takes. We don't want to rush it. Are you both getting tired? Maybe another cookie? And then, a bit of quiet reading time before dinner? Speaker_2: More cookie, please! Speaker_3: Rest! Then pirate stories! Speaker_1: You got it. (Starts texting) Right, Fiona... "Tuesday for coffee? Would love to catch up! Let me know…" Oh, and have you two thought about haircuts? Your hair is getting a bit long. We could book something in for next month. Speaker_2: No haircut! I like my hair! Speaker_3: Long hair! Like a pirate! Speaker_1: (Sighs, playfully) Of course, you do! Alright, alright, we’ll discuss it later. No forcing haircuts. Just thinking ahead. And I was hoping we could try that new chocolate cake recipe this weekend. It uses three different kinds of chocolate. Speaker_2: Chocolate cake! Yummy! Speaker_3: Cake! Cake! Chocolate! Speaker_1: Yes, lots of chocolate! Everything is getting a bit chocolatey, isn’t it? Now, let’s have a proper story time. Which book shall we choose?

Speaker_1: (Sipping her iced latte, looking slightly exasperated) Honestly, this queue is ridiculous. I’ve been stood here for like, ten minutes already. What are people even ordering? It’s just sandwiches! Speaker_2: (Chuckles, already halfway through a wrap) Tell me about it! I came a bit earlier, thinking I'd beat the rush, but nope. University canteen logic. You getting your usual? Speaker_1: Yeah, the iced latte and a chicken and pesto sandwich. Gotta keep the energy up for that dreadful lecture this afternoon. Professor Davies is just… enthusiastic. In a draining way. Speaker_2: (grimaces sympathetically) Oh, Davies. Don’t remind me. I had him last year for Intro to Contemporary Literature. The PowerPoint presentations alone were enough to make me want to drop out. Remember that one with all the Comic Sans? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh my god, yes! It was like a fever dream. Seriously, who uses Comic Sans in a university lecture? Speaker_2: I know, right? Anyway, what are you up to after this, then? Thought we might actually *do* something this weekend. Something involving not lectures. Speaker_1: I was thinking about that! My mate Liam’s throwing a little pre-club get-together at his flat on Saturday. Nothing massive, just drinks and music. Fancy coming? Speaker_2: Ooh, sounds good! Whereabouts is he? Is it a trek? I'm still a little dodgy after that dodgy kebab I had on Tuesday. My stomach’s been playing up all week. My Nan would kill me if she knew I ate somewhere that wasn't thoroughly checked for cleanliness. She's a right stickler. Speaker_1: It's not too bad. Richmond, actually. We could grab the train. And a dodgy kebab? Girl, you are brave. I’d rather eat sawdust. Speaker_2: Brave or foolish? Jury’s still out on that one. But it was cheap, and I was starving. Anyway, Richmond, yeah, I can deal with that. What kind of music are we talking? Anything I should prepare myself for? Liam's taste is… eclectic. Speaker_1: (Smiling wryly) He's got a penchant for 90s rave and obscure Turkish pop music. Don't ask. Just… be prepared. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Right, noted. Rave and Turkish pop. That's a combo I never anticipated experiencing. Anything decent to eat at Liam's, or just crisps and dips? Because I am *still* recovering from the kebab situation. Speaker_1: He usually puts on a decent spread. Last time there was nachos, pizza, and even some proper homemade brownies. He’s trying to impress someone. Speaker_2: (Raises an eyebrow) Ooh, mystery girl? Spill the tea! Who’s the lucky lady? Speaker_1: Apparently, a girl from his photography class. She's supposed to be quite arty and cool. He's absolutely smitten. Keeps calling her his 'muse'. It’s adorable and slightly embarrassing. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Classic Liam. Okay, I’m definitely in then. So, Saturday, Richmond, rave, Turkish pop, potential brownie consumption... Sounds like a plan! What about you? Anything exciting happening your end? Apart from facing the wrath of Professor Davies, obviously. Speaker_1: Not really, just trying to survive uni at the moment. I'm thinking of re-applying for that internship at the gallery, though. It would look great on my CV. Speaker_2: You should! You'd be brilliant there! You've always had such an eye for detail. Proper star, you are. Oh! Speaking of detail, did you hear about Chloe accidentally setting off the fire alarm in the library yesterday? Speaker_1: No way! What happened? Speaker_2: Apparently, she was trying to heat up leftovers in a microwave that wasn't supposed to be used. Apparently, it went up in a lot of smoke! The whole place had to be evacuated

Speaker_1: (Sipping tea, grimacing slightly) Right, this Earl Grey is a bit… intense, isn't it? Like someone’s tried to brew a sock in it. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, adjusting his glasses) A sock? That's… descriptive, Elsie. It’s alright, I think. More flavour than that builder's tea you normally drink, anyway. Speaker_3: (Smiling, leaning back on the sofa) He's got a point there, Elsie. You’re used to that pale, comforting beige. This is actually *tea*. Anyway, so, tell us about this trip to the Lakes you were planning. Sounds absolutely gorgeous. Speaker_1: Aye, it does sound grand, doesn’t it? Still stuck on trying to figure out the logistics though. The train times are a nightmare, and finding somewhere that doesn't cost a fortune is proving difficult. I was lookin’ at a little cottage near Keswick. It was cute, but the reviews mentioned, and I quote, “persistent mice.” Not exactly the relaxing getaway I was hopin’ for. Speaker_2: Keswick is brilliant! We went there years ago with my family. Stunning scenery. The mice thing, though... yeah, that’s not ideal. Have you looked at Bowness-on-Windermere? Maybe a bit pricier, but you might get lucky. I’ve got a contact at a holiday letting agency, actually. Let me have a poke around. Speaker_3: That's really kind of you, Finn. Elsie, Bowness *is* lovely, a bit busier than Keswick, admittedly. But plenty of nice pubs and things to do. Have you seen the new series of “The Responder” on BBC? Speaker_1: “The Responder”? No, what’s that like? Is it grim? 'Cause I've had enough grim in my life, thanks very much. My work alone is a constant barrage of grammatical errors and erratic punctuation. I’m a Corpus Administrator, for heaven's sake! People can’t even spell “the” correctly these days. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, Elsie! You're a saint. "The Responder" is brilliant, actually. Martin Freeman's in it. It’s a police procedural, but it's set in Liverpool, during a blizzard. Really gritty and dark humour. You'd like the bleakness. Speaker_3: Definitely bleak, but in a good way. It's expertly written, and the acting is superb. It's not all doom and gloom though, there's some genuine human connection there. Actually, speaking of connections, have you tried that new Indian place, “Spice Route”, down the road? Speaker_1: No, I haven't! I’ve been meaning to, though. My mam raves about it. Says they do a proper vindaloo. Proper hot, not that watered-down nonsense you get in some places. Speaker_2: Spice Route is amazing! I took my mum there last week. The butter chicken was divine. Seriously, you have to go. We could all go next week, maybe? After your Lakes planning saga. Speaker_3: I'm in! Elsie, are you thinking of coming along? It would be a nice change from mice and erratic punctuation. Speaker_1: (Grinning) Alright, alright, you've twisted my arm. A nice curry sounds perfect. As long as there are no rogue rodents lurking in the kitchen. So, Finn, you’ll have a look at those cottages for me then? Anything near a decent pub would be a bonus. And tell me, what’s this holiday letting agency you know? Do they do discounts for perpetually-stressed Corpus Administrators? Speaker_2: (Chuckling) I'll see what I can do about the discount. Let's not get our hopes up, though, these agencies are ruthless. But I’ll definitely have a look. And Tom (Speaker_3), you’ve got to tell me more about this series. Sounds like exactly what I need after wading through bridge designs all day. A good dose of bleakness.

Speaker_1: (Sipping tea, looking out the window) Lovely bit o’ sunshine we’re havin’ today, innit? Reminds me of that trip we took to Norfolk when I were a lad. Remember the horses on the common? Proper shying things, they were. Speaker_2: (Smiling warmly) Oh, I do, Arthur. Though I was thinking more of that awful rain we had in Cornwall last year. Remember that youth hostel? Damp as a dishrag! Still, the scenery was spectacular, wasn't it? Though I'm not sure young Colin appreciated being soaked through. Speaker_3: (Entering the room, carrying a stack of papers) Cornwall was alright, yes. A bit chilly for my liking though. I’m just sorting out some forms, dealing with a bit of admin at school. Speaker_1: (Slumping onto a beanbag chair, letting out a long sigh) Blimey, this place is cozy, innit? Zara’s got good taste, I gotta say. Though I’ve always enjoyed looking after the children, even when it was all a bit much. But the solitary nature of it, you know? Getting old on your own... It’s hard. Speaker_1: Aye. Hard. (He pauses, fidgeting with the corner of his teacup). I’ve just... I’ve just not been one for change, I suppose. Been here for forty years now, in this flat. Plenty of memories. Mostly not good ones, mind you. Speaker_3: I understand, Arthur. But memories are just that – memories. This is about building new ones. A place where you can relax, have some peace and quiet, and actually enjoy your retirement. Think of all the walks you could take along the river! Speaker_2: (Smiling gently) He’s right, Arthur. No more worrying about the heating bill, no more struggling to reach the top shelves. We could even have a little book club, maybe? I’ve always fancied that. Speaker_1: A book club? Cor, Margaret. Don't get carried away. Though… (He considers it, a faint smile playing on his lips.) I did quite enjoy "The Wind in the Willows," back in the day. Speaker_3: See? A glimmer of enthusiasm! Mine are the same. “Get a sensible job, save your money, buy a flat.” But what’s the point of saving for a flat if you’re miserable in the process? I don’t want to look back in twenty years and think, “I should have taken that chance.” Speaker_2: Exactly! That’s exactly how I feel. It's just... there's so much uncertainty. What if I’m terrible at it? What if it doesn’t pay well? What if I end up regretting it even more? Speaker_1: Look, no one knows the future. But you’re smart, you’re creative, and you've got a good eye. If you’re passionate about it, you're more likely to succeed, right? And even if you don't become the next Kelly Hoppen, it’ll still be a fulfilling change. Maybe start small? A weekend course? Just to see if you actually enjoy it? Speaker_2: That's… a really good idea. A small step feels much less terrifying than a giant leap. I could look into those weekend pottery classes too, just for kicks. You know, to rule it out properly. Speaker_1: (Grinning) Exactly! Rule it out with artistic flair. Besides, you never know – you might surprise yourself. And who knows, maybe we’ll both be living our dream lives in a few years. You, designing beautiful homes, me, filming documentaries in the Amazon… Speaker_

Speaker_1: (Sighs dramatically, swirling the straw in her brightly coloured drink) Honestly, I'm *fuming*. Absolutely fuming. Speaker_2: (Leaning back in her chair, sunglasses perched on her nose) Ooh, what now, Liv? What’s set you off this time? Him again? Speaker_1: It's not just *him*, Rach. It’s… everything. He was all over Chloe at the market this morning. Like, genuinely. Chatting her up, laughing at her stupid jokes… I could practically feel my eyeballs popping out of my head. Speaker_3: (Looking up from her sketchbook, a slightly bemused expression on her face) Chloe? Chloe who works at the bakery? The one who dyes her hair bright pink? Speaker_1: Aye, that’s her. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Liv, you’re being ridiculous. He’s just being polite. You’re being a right drama queen. Speaker_1: Easy for you to say, you’ve been single since… well, forever! You don't know the sting of being stood up for, Rach. It’s not about politeness, it's about respect. And he’s not showing me any. Speaker_3: Rach's got a point, Liv. Men are generally… less demonstrative. Especially when they're trying to be agreeable to everyone. Remember when Tom kept complimenting Sarah’s earrings at your cousin's wedding? Didn't mean he was leaving you. Speaker_1: (Grumbling) Tom was a creep. And this is different. This felt… intentional. He was deliberately trying to wind me up. I swear, if he does it again... I might just chuck his phone in the Seine. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Now *that* would be entertainment! Don't do anything drastic, Liv. How about we just forget about him for a bit? Paris is lovely. Enjoy the macarons, the sunshine… live a little. Speaker_1: I’m trying! But it's hard when you’re constantly thinking about being replaced by a woman with neon pink hair and a passion for pain au chocolat. Speaker_3: You're not being replaced, Liv. You're overthinking. He probably just likes chatting to people. Remember what my mum always says? "Don’t sweat the small stuff, and everything else doesn’t matter." Speaker_1: Your mum also says that floral wallpaper is *always* a good choice. Her advice isn’t always golden, Izzy. Speaker_2: She does have a point, though, doesn’t she? Besides, haven't you been moaning about wanting a bit of excitement in your life? This is your excitement. Speaker_1: My excitement shouldn’t involve feeling like I’m competing for a bloke's affections! Honestly, I wish I'd stayed home and watched reruns of 'Coronation Street'. At least then I'd know where I stood. Speaker_3: Right, new topic. I saw the cutest little vintage shop earlier. We absolutely *have* to go. We could find some incredible treasures. Speaker_2: Ooh, I'm in! A bit of retail therapy is exactly what we need. Liv, agree? Distract yourself with a ridiculous beret. Speaker_1: (Hesitates, then a small smile appears) Alright, alright. A beret might help. But if I see him flirting with Chloe again, I'm blaming you two for my eventual breakdown. Speaker_2: Deal. Now, let's find that shop! And maybe a giant éclair. Speaker_3: (Standing up) Lead the way! Just try not to picture him with pink hair while we're looking. We’ve got Parisian adventures to conquer!

Speaker_1: (Reaching for a bread roll) This shepherd's pie is absolutely lovely, isn't it? Honestly, Mark, you’ve outdone yourself. Speaker_3: (Smiling proudly) Cheers, Sarah. Glad you like it. Though, I reckon a bit more gravy wouldn’t go amiss. Speaker_4: (Nodding enthusiastically) Yeah, more gravy would be brilliant! I’m still starving. Hockey’s made me ravenous. Speaker_1: Hockey? How did your game go, Liam? You seemed pretty fired up when you left. Speaker_4: It was intense! We lost by one goal, though. Heartbreaking, really. Got a couple of decent tackles in. Coach said I was covering a lot of ground. So, yeah, not too bad. Speaker_2: (Looking up from his plate) Did you see that save from Ben? Amazing! He practically pulled it out of the air. Speaker_1: Oh, Ben’s the goalkeeper, right? He's always been a good one. Remember that time he saved that penalty in the regional finals? Speaker_3: (Chuckling) Ah, yes! Good times. Speaking of good times, Sarah, we should finally book that trip to Cornwall. Remember we talked about going last summer? Speaker_1: (Her face lighting up) Cornwall! Absolutely! I’ve been looking at some cottages online. There's a gorgeous one in St. Ives, right by the harbour. It’s a bit pricier, but the pictures are just stunning. Speaker_2: Cornwall? Can we go surfing?! Please, Dad, please?! Speaker_3: (Laughing) We'll see, Jamie. Surfing depends on the weather, and your enthusiasm! But it’s definitely on the cards. We could even visit the Eden Project. Speaker_4: Eden Project? Sounds…educational. I’d rather go climbing somewhere. Speaker_1: (To Liam) There are some fantastic climbing spots in Cornwall, love. The south coast is riddled with them! Maybe we can factor that in. Speaker_3: Right, so Cornwall it is then. Let's look at dates. Sarah, when are you free in the next few months? Speaker_1: Let me check my diary… Hmm, June looks a bit tight with that marketing project, but July looks good. Or even late August. Speaker_2: July! That's when the new FIFA game comes out! I’ll need internet access for that, obviously. Speaker_3: (Rolling his eyes playfully) Naturally. The world revolves around FIFA, doesn’t it? Speaker_4: (Grinning) It does! And I need to practice my new skills. I've been trying this new formation… Speaker_1: (Smiling at the scene) It’s lovely to see you all so enthusiastic. All these plans are so exciting. It feels like ages since we've had a proper family holiday. Speaker_3: It has been a while. Needed a bit of a recharge, didn't we? So, Cornwall – cottages, surfing, Eden Project, climbing… Anything else we should add to the list? Speaker_2: Ice cream! Lots and lots of ice cream! Speaker_4: And a really good pub. Somewhere with proper fish and chips. Speaker_1: (Laughing) You two are incorrigible! I'll start looking at those cottages seriously then. St. Ives it is, I think. Speaker_3: Excellent. Let’s get this organised. It’ll be brilliant. And maybe, just maybe, this time I'll manage to relax for once.

Speaker_1: (Looking out the window, a slight smile on her face) Honestly, this is breathtaking, isn’t it? I didn't realise trees could get *this* big. It feels… prehistoric. Like something out of Jurassic Park. Speaker_2: (Leaning back against the seat, scrolling through her phone briefly, then looking up) It really is. Though, I'm not sure a T-Rex would appreciate being hemmed in by all this greenery. My neck hurts just looking up! Did you see that tiny little hummingbird earlier? It was zipping about. Speaker_2: (Putting her phone down completely) Nope, still nothing concrete. She mumbled something about "logistics" and "venue availability." You know Sarah – she specialises in making things unnecessarily complicated. I suspect it's because Mark still hasn’t fully committed to learning the tango. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Oh, Mark. Poor Mark. He looks like he'd rather wrestle a bear than attempt a tango. He insists he’s “rhythmically challenged.” Speaker_2: Rhythmically challenged is putting it gently. Remember his attempt at karaoke at Liam’s birthday? He tried to sing Bohemian Rhapsody and… well, let’s just say the microphone deserved a medal. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, bless him. He’s got enthusiasm, I'll give him that. But the actual singing? Definitely not his forte. I feel sorry for Sarah, though. She’s always wanted this big, romantic wedding. Speaker_2: I do too. She deserves it. She’s been working so hard. What about your mum? Has she booked her flights yet? I know she was dithering about the cost. Speaker_1: She’s booked! Surprisingly. She used those frequent flyer miles she's been hoarding for years. Apparently, she managed to snag a decent deal. She’s already planning all her outfits, naturally. Five, she says, "one for each day of the celebrations." Speaker_2: (Smiling) Typical Mum. She’ll be bringing enough floral prints to single-handedly brighten up the entire Californian coast. Are you worried about Uncle David and his… tendencies? Speaker_1: (Grimaces slightly) Let's just say I’ve briefed Mark on the "Uncle David protocol." Which is, essentially, keep him away from open bars and strategically positioned to be near someone who can discreetly steer him towards water. Speaker_2: (Nods knowingly) Wise move. Remember that incident at Christmas with the inflatable reindeer? Still gives me nightmares. Although, I have to admit, his rendition of “Silent Night” after several glasses of sherry was… memorable. Speaker_1: Memorable is one word for it. I’m mostly just relieved Grandma isn’t going to witness it this time. She’d have a coronary. She still talks about the time he tried to convince her he was a visiting dignitary from Liechtenstein. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, Grandma! She’s so wonderfully gullible. But then again, she *is* 87. It’s allowed. I'm just hoping to have some downtime on this trip. I've been doing so much temp work lately, I need a proper break. Speaker_1: Absolutely. We all do. California seems like the perfect antidote to a stressful few months. Although, I might need to invest in a neck brace after staring at these redwood giants for too long. Seriously, they’re enormous! Do you think they've always been this big? Speaker_2: I imagine so. They've probably been quietly growing for hundreds of years while we've been busy squabbling over karaoke and inflatable reindeer. Let’s just appreciate it, shall we? And maybe book a massage for both of us when we get back. Speaker_1: Deal. A very big deal indeed.

Speaker_1: (Reaching for a biscuit) Ah, these are good. Proper dunkers, these. Not like those flimsy ones you get nowadays. Did you lads enjoy the Kievs? I think I might’ve gone a bit heavy on the garlic, myself. Speaker_2: (Mouth full) Yeah, they were alright, Dad. Bit garlicky, maybe. But better than last time, when they were dry as dust. We're talking about Granny and Leo. Did you check on the Dropbox folder for the photos I sent over of the toddler? I need to show Granny when she's here. And could you remind Leo to back them up on Flickr as well? I hate losing photos. Speaker_2: Flicker? Dropbox? Mum, you’re such a tech head. Honestly. Can't you just print them? Speaker_1: See what I mean? Leo needs to learn about cloud storage. Essential in this day and age. It’s like having a safety net for your memories, isn't it? Speaking of safety, did you see that rugby match yesterday? Absolutely brutal! Those lads are taking some serious hits. Gave me a headache just watching it. Speaker_3: Tell me about it! It’s good for her, getting visitors. Though I wonder if the hedgehog is still getting into the garden. I saw tracks again last night. Speaker_2: (Eyes widen) A hedgehog?! Really? Can I see it? Speaker_1: Now, now, Leo, leave the poor creature alone. They’re just looking for a bit of food. Like all of us, I suppose. Another biscuit then? I think I deserve one after all this talk of rugby, garlic, and hedgehogs.

Speaker_1: (Stirring a pot vigorously) Honestly, David, I’m still buzzing about that set of Shelley cups and saucers I snagged on eBay. Can you believe the price? Fifty quid! For Shelley! Speaker_2: (Chopping vegetables at the counter) Fifty quid? You're having me on. Shelley's usually commands a far higher price, even with imperfections. Let me see a picture. (He pulls out his phone) Speaker_1: (Walking over to show him) Right here. See? A tiny hairline crack on one saucer, but otherwise, they’re exquisite. The floral pattern is just... *chef’s kiss*. Think of the afternoon teas we can have! Speaker_2: (Squinting at the phone) Right, right, fair enough. A hairline crack does make a difference. Still, a steal. You’ve got a knack for finding these things, you know. Like that Royal Worcester teapot last year. Speaker_1: It's a talent! Though it does occasionally require a small fortune in postage. Speaking of finding things, I’m thinking of trying that buckwheat bread recipe I saw. You know, the one with the sunflower seeds? Speaker_2: Buckwheat bread? Sounds…interesting. Not usually my go-to. Is it very difficult? My baking skills are, shall we say, rudimentary. Speaker_1: Not at all! It's surprisingly easy, and supposedly very good for you. Plus, I need something to go with that lovely Stilton I picked up at the market yesterday. It'll be a proper treat. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You and your markets! You come back laden with cheese and antique china. I swear, you could open a little shop. And I'd be stuck washing up mountains of teacups. Speaker_1: Don’t be such a grump! It’s the community spirit, David. You should join me more often. It's brilliant for meeting people and finding all sorts of interesting things. Speaker_2: I'm happy weeding the garden, thank you very much. Besides, I've got that leaving do to organise for Sarah next week. It’s proving to be rather more complicated than I anticipated. People have *opinions* about music and food apparently. Speaker_1: Oh, yes, Sarah’s leaving. It's no good to her, is it? She deserved a promotion. You'll get it sorted though. You're a master organizer. Have you decided on a venue? Speaker_2: We’re leaning towards The Old Mill. It’s got a nice atmosphere, and they do decent canapés. But securing the space on a Friday evening in this town is like pulling teeth. Everyone wants a party. Speaker_1: You’ll manage. Just delegate! That’s what you’re good at. Don't try to do everything yourself. And have you finalised the guest list? Are you inviting Clive from accounts? Speaker_2: (Grimaces) Ugh, Clive. Yes, sadly. Office politics demands it, I’m afraid. He insists on playing his 'motivational' speakers on the sound system. I'm strategically placing myself far, far away from the speakers. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, David! You have to be firm with him. Tell him nobody wants to hear Tony Robbins whilst eating vol-au-vents. Back to supper though, I’m wondering if we have any apple sauce? That buckwheat could take it. Speaker_2: I think there's a jar in the fridge. Though, truth be told, I’m secretly hoping you make enough bread for a proper sandwich tomorrow. I fancy a cheese and tomato on buckwheat. Speaker_1: (Smiling) See? I knew you’d come around. You’ll be a convert to buckwheat bread in no time. I'll save you a slice. Now, help me set the table – we need to admire those new cups and saucers properly.

Speaker_4: (Sipping espresso, looking relaxed) ...and honestly, the paperwork alone for this latest client is enough to drive a person mad. It's all about offshore accounts these days, isn't it? Seems everyone wants to… shield themselves. Speaker_1: (Wrinkling her nose, Yorkshire accent thick) Shield themselves, aye? Sounds a bit dodgy, don't it, Uncle Dave? I’m studying law now, remember? We’re learning about money laundering and all that. It’s proper scary stuff, innit? Speaker_2: (Calmly, Eastern English accent) Don’t be dramatic, Maisie. It's complicated financial regulation, not necessarily criminal activity. There’s perfectly legitimate reasons for international banking. My business operates across several borders, you know. Requires a bit of careful structuring. Speaker_3: (Leaning back, mumbled Yorkshire accent) 'Structuring'… yeah, that’s a good word for it. Keeps things neat. Speaker_4: (Chuckles lightly) Liam’s got a point. It *is* complicated, Lucy. And there’s always a grey area. My job is to navigate that grey area. Legally, of course. Mostly. Look, this client… he’s a property developer. Big developments in Spain, some in Dubai. He’s paying hefty fines over in France for some building code violations. Seems he cut a few corners. Proper mess, really. Speaker_1: Fines? Like, how much? And building code violations... sounds like someone got greedy. Speaker_2: (Raises an eyebrow at Maisie) Greedy’s a harsh word. Sometimes ambition clashes with bureaucracy. It happens. What sort of fines are we talking about, Dave? And what’s the structure you’re setting up to help him? Don't get too technical, though, I'm not a chartered accountant. Speaker_4: Well, the fines initially totalled over €500,000. We’ve managed to negotiate that down to around €350,000, but it still stings. The key is moving assets… intelligently. We’re using a series of shell companies in the Cayman Islands, moving funds through various brokerage accounts... it’s a delicate dance, really. Has to look… organic. Speaker_3: (Suddenly interested) Shell companies, eh? Like, invisible companies? That’s clever. Speaker_2: Liam! Don't encourage him. Uncle Dave, are you absolutely certain this is… wise? We’ve talked about your conscience before. Remember that trip to the Lake District and the guilt you felt after that newspaper article about those dodgy tax schemes? Speaker_4: (Waves a dismissive hand) Lucy, darling, that was years ago. I'm much more discerning now. Besides, this is a service I’m providing. He's paying very well for it. And I’m very good at what I do. I wasn’t involved in the initial violations, I’m just cleaning up the mess. That’s a very important distinction. Speaker_1: (Shivers slightly) It still sounds a bit… wrong. What if you get caught? Serious trouble, like, prison trouble? Speaker_4: (Laughs heartily) Maisie, you worry too much. The banks are our allies in this. They handle the transactions, they’re the ones who bear the brunt of the consequences if anything goes south. As long as I'm careful, meticulous... I’m fine. Think of it as a complex game of chess. Speaker_2: (Sighs) Chess with potentially devastating consequences. That’s what worries me. What about the kids, Dave? What legacy are you leaving them? Speaker_4: (Looks a bit uncomfortable) The kids are provided for, Lucy. They don't need to worry about anything. And they’ll appreciate the security, eventually. Besides, this pays for their future schooling, doesn’t it? Speaker_3: (Grinning) Future schooling. Fancy universities, then? Speaker_1: (Glares at Liam) This is all about money, isn’t it?

Speaker_3: (Smiling brightly, stirring sugar into her coffee) Honestly, this weather is mad, isn't it? One minute sunshine, the next a proper downpour. The kids were gutted - we’d planned a nature walk this morning, but it was just a soggy mess. Speaker_1: (Chuckling softly) Tell me about it, love. I was hoping to get a bit of gardening done, but it’s been on and off all day. At least the rain's good for the garden in the long run, I suppose. Though I am starting to miss decent sunshine. Speaker_2: (Taking a slow sip of his coffee) It’s typical, isn’t it? Just when you think you've got a nice spell of weather, the heavens open. Still, beats a snowstorm, I reckon. Remember that one a few years back? Couldn’t get out for days. Speaker_4: (Laughing) Oh my god, the traffic was insane! I was stuck on the A38 for, like, three hours. I was bringing back a huge delivery for the store, and everything just ground to a halt. Absolute chaos! We finally got it through, but it was touch and go for a while. Speaker_3: Speaking of chaos, how's the store doing, Chloe? Still busy? Speaker_4: Ridiculously busy. It’s the run-up to Christmas, you know? Non-stop. Honestly, the energy levels are draining. But the team’s pulling together. We’re trying to keep spirits up with hot chocolate breaks and cheesy Christmas music. Speaker_1: Well, you've got to embrace the madness, haven't you? Is it all geared up for the big day then? Decorations and all? Speaker_4: Absolutely! We’ve got the full works. Giant inflatable reindeer, flashing lights, the whole shebang. It’s a bit much, maybe, but people seem to like it. Speaker_2: (Grumbling good-naturedly) Too much, definitely too much. My ears are ringing already just thinking about it. All that tinsel… Speaker_3: (Teasingly) Oh, don't be such a grump, David! Christmas wouldn't be Christmas without a bit of over-the-top festivity. Anyway, changing the subject slightly… I've been thinking about signing up for that sign language class. Speaker_1: Really? That's lovely, darling! Where is it, then? Speaker_3: It’s at the community centre down the road. It's a beginners' course, so hopefully, I'll pick it up quickly. I thought it'd be useful, you know, especially with the baby coming. It could be useful for communicating with her if she’s upset, or something. Speaker_4: That’s a really good idea, Amy! I reckon it’s brilliant. Plus, it's just a really useful skill to have. Speaker_2: (Nodding slowly) Aye, that's sensible. Always good to pick up new things. Though, honestly, I doubt I’d ever manage it. My coordination isn't exactly top-notch, you know. Speaker_1: Don't be silly, you could give it a go! It might surprise you. We could all go to the classes together for support, couldn't we? It'd be a bit of family time. Speaker_3: That would be amazing! Imagine us all signing Christmas carols! Speaker_4: (Laughing) I'd love that! Though David would probably get all the signs mixed up. Speaker_2: (Feigning offense) Hey! I resent that! Speaker_1: (Smiling) Alright, alright! Back to more important matters. How’s everything going with the baby prep? Any signs of… movement? Speaker_3: Actually, yes! I felt her kick properly for the first time yesterday. It was the sweetest thing. Absolutely magical. Speaker_4: Oh, Amy! That’s wonderful news! You must be so excited! When’s the scan, again?

Good to see you all actually managed to find a table, though. It’s usually a battle. Speaker_4: (With a wry smile) Tell me about it. I nearly had to wrestle Sarah from Accounts for this spot. It needs a bit of seasoning, maybe some lemon. And you're not wrong about the light, Elin. I swear I turn paler by the day just working here. So, did anyone manage to get through the proofs for the Dickens biography? Speaker_3: (Wrinkling her nose) Tried. But honestly, the footnotes alone are a beast. Professor Harding expects *everything* documented to the nth degree. I think I aged five years just reading one chapter. Speaker_1: (Nodding sympathetically) Oh, Harding! He's a force of nature. Are you finding anything particularly interesting, Chloe? Speaker_2: (Shrugs) Just a lot of minor factual errors. Dates don’t quite match, places are misattributed… the usual. It’s tedious but someone’s gotta do it. The sheer volume of material he dealt with is staggering, though, isn't it? Speaker_4: (Sipping her water) It's wild to think about how much went into all those books. All the editing, the proofreading, the typesetting… and now, everything’s digital. It feels… impersonal somehow. Like there’s less care. Speaker_3: I disagree slightly. I think the sheer speed means there’s potentially *more* care, just spread out differently. We catch things digitally that would have slipped through a typist in the Victorian era. It's just a different kind of rigor. Plus, think of the trees we're saving! Speaker_1: That's a solid point, Mei. Though, there’s a certain romance to the physicality of a well-crafted book that’s hard to replicate. That feeling when you open a first edition and the smell… pure magic. Speaker_2: (Raises an eyebrow) You sound like you’re about to write a poem about old books, Amelia. Speaker_1: (Laughs) Don’t tempt me! It’s a very real phenomenon. It's why my research focuses on the evolution of language in printed texts. It’s not just about the words themselves, but the entire physical experience of reading. Speaker_4: So, like, you’re analysing the psychology of book ownership? That’s fascinating! I've been thinking a lot about how the design and layout of a book impacts the reader. Do you have opinions on font choices? Speaker_1: Oh, absolutely! Garamond is eternally stylish, obviously. But so much depends on the context – the size, the weight, the era it’s meant to evoke… it’s a surprisingly complex interaction. Anyone got a favourite font? Speaker_2: Times New Roman. Practical, legible. Gets the job done. No fuss. Speaker_3: (Scoffs playfully) So predictable, Chloe! I’m partial to Baskerville. It’s got a refined elegance, don't you think? Speaker_4: I'm a fan of Futura. Modern, clean, it feels… optimistic. Though, honestly, I'm just happy if I can read it without straining my eyes after spending eight hours staring at a screen. Speaker_1: (Slumping onto ANON's sofa, letting out a long sigh) Right, so, Mongolia. Still feels a bit mental when I say it out loud, doesn't it? Speaker_1: (Sighs dramatically, leaning her head against the car window) Honestly, this drive feels like it's lasting a lifetime. Are we nearly there yet, love? My neck's killin' me. A bit of a lighter moment to balance out all the sadness? Speaker_1: (A small smile spreads across her face) Actually, there was. Your cousin, little Thomas… bless him. I could do it, no bother. I’m alright with computers, you know, bein' a corpus administrator and all. Just need a bit of time and space. Speaker_2: See? You’re incredible. All that attention to detail, the way you organise things… you’d be perfect for it. And it’ll give you something practical you can do to help, instead of just feeling helpless. Speaker_1: You’re right. I’ll offer it to her tomorrow. She'll be chuffed, I reckon. It's just… sometimes, I wish I could just wave a magic wand and make all the hurt go away. Speaker_2: (Reaches over and squeezes her hand gently) Me too, lass. Me too. But sometimes just being there, listening, and offering a small act

Speaker_3: (Sipping her tea, looking out the window) Honestly, this rain is relentless. It's been chucking it down for days now. Feels like Norfolk is permanently under water. Speaker_1: (Grunts, stirring sugar into his tea with a deliberate slowness) Aye, it's a bit of a soggy business, innit? Remember '78? Now *that* was a summer. Sun blazin', barely a cloud in the sky. Speaker_4: (Leaning back in his chair, scrolling through his phone) You know, weather apps are getting surprisingly accurate these days. They predicted this downpour down to the minute. Always wanted stories about dragons and knights instead. Speaker_1: Dragons, eh? Used to tell young’uns stories myself, back when…well, never you mind. Still, the football's on tonight. Norwich are playing Ipswich. Should be a good match, even in this weather. Speaker_4: (Looks up from his phone) Ipswich? Really? Figured Norwich would have a better chance. Any bets? Speaker_3: Absolutely not. I have lectures to grade and a research paper to finish. I can’t afford to get emotionally invested in something as unpredictable as football. Besides, Daniel would just bore us all with stats. Speaker_4: Hey! I just enjoy analysing the probabilities. It’s…intellectually stimulating. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Oh, Daniel. Always with the big words. You and your fancy degrees. Still can’t boil an egg properly, though. Speaker_4: That’s a blatant exaggeration. Speaker_1: (Chuckles, a dry, wheezing sound) Don’t let her wind you up, lad. Women and their cheek. Reminds me of my Doris…always nippin’ at me. Still miss her, though. Speaker_3: (Softening slightly) I know you do, Arthur. It's been a long time. Have you been taking your medication regularly? You seemed a little…out of sorts last week. Speaker_1: Aye, I’m alright, love. Just a bit of a creak in the old bones. The doctor says it's the rain, plays havoc with the joints, he says. Nonsense, I reckon. More likely it's this dreadful tea. Needs a good strong brew, this. Speaker_2: Now, Arthur, don't you start complaining about ANON’s tea. It's lovely! And you know perfectly well the doctor told you to take it easy. You can't be pacing around the garden in this weather. You'll catch your death. Speaker_4: Speaking of health, I’ve been looking at these new smartwatches, the ones that monitor your heart rate and sleep. They’re surprisingly advanced. Thought maybe you’d be interested, Arthur? Speaker_1: A whatchamacallit? Thing on your wrist? Sounds like a load of fuss. Give me a good cup of tea and a sit down any day. All this modern technology is just too much bother. Besides, I can feel when I need a sit down, can’t I? Speaker_3: It could be useful, though. To keep track of things. You just never know what’s lurking just below the surface

Speaker_3: (Sipping her wine, leaning back on the sofa) Honestly, this week has been mental. Mr. Henderson wants *everything* redesigned for the new brochure. Everything! I’m dealing with spreadsheets and targets all day. At least *my* ridiculousness is financially rewarding. Though, don’t get me wrong, the pressure is on. Big sales push next month. Speaker_4: (Waving a hand dismissively) Sales, spreadsheets… sounds easy comparatively to Mr. Henderson's artistic whims. Remember last year when he decided all the corporate colours needed to be ‘evocative of a sunset’? Speaker_3: (Groaning) Don’t remind me. Remember my dad's face when I told him I wanted neon green accents in my flat? He nearly had a stroke. Speaker_3: (Chuckling) Right? Parents. They're just… there to worry. So, when’s the actual date? Any narrowing down? Speaker_2: June 15th! Feels so real now. Although, I’m starting to get a bit… twitchy about the whole “marriage” thing. It’s just… a big commitment, you know? Speaker_1: Of course it is! It's terrifying, isn’t it? But a good one is wonderful. My aunt and uncle have been married for… goodness, 45 years? They're still ridiculously in love. Speaker_4: My nan always says the secret is separate bathrooms. Speaker_3: (Laughing) Wise woman, your nan. Seriously though, Liv, you seem happy. That's the most important thing. Speaker_2: I am. Mostly. It’s just… people keep asking about kids. Like, it’s the next logical step. Do you guys want kids? Speaker_1: Eventually, maybe. Definitely not right now. I'm still figuring out how to keep a houseplant alive. Speaker_4: I'm firmly in the “absolutely not” camp. Too much responsibility. I like my freedom and my sleep. Speaker_3: Same here. I’d probably forget to feed them. Or accidentally dress them in Mr. Henderson’s sunset-inspired colour palette. Speaker_2: (Smiling) You’re all terrible influences. But it's good to hear. Makes me feel a bit less pressured. It's my life, isn’t it? We shouldn't have to have it all figured out. Speaker_1: Exactly! So, what about a change of subject? Anyone been seeing anyone interesting? Spill the tea! Speaker_4: Actually, yeah! Remember Mark from university? The graphic design one? Speaker_3: Vaguely… was he the one with the woolly hat, even in summer? Speaker_4: That's the one! He just messaged me. Turns out he’s back in Peterborough. Said he’d love to grab a coffee. Speaker_2: Ooh! Get me the details! He sounds promising. Although, beware the woolly hat. Could be a sign of questionable fashion sense.

Speaker_1: (Sipping tea, grimacing slightly) This newfangled kettle, eh? Whirls about like a fairground ride it does. Never had one like it in me life. Too complicated, I reckon. Give me a good old gas stove any day. You remember those, Marjorie? Proper heat you got! Speaker_2: (Chuckles, stirring her tea) Oh, I do, Arthur. Though, honestly, I preferred electric. A bit less faff, no soot everywhere. Though yours *was* always a bit temperamental, wasn't it? Remember that time it nearly blew the lights out at Christmas? Your Maggie nearly had a heart attack! Speaker_3: (Smiling warmly) I remember! I was just a teenager then, visiting for the holidays. It was quite the scene. Speaking of Christmas, my workload before retirement always peaked around that time. Marking essays, planning nativity plays... it was relentless. Did you ever have many children at yours, Marjorie? Speaker_2: Oh, bless you, David. Loads! I ran a childminding business for years, just after Matthew left for university. A constant stream of little ones. Some were absolute angels, some… well, let's just say they kept me on my toes! Little Rosie, bless her, used to try and feed the goldfish toast. Every. Single. Day. Speaker_1: (Lets out a wheezy chuckle) Kids, eh? They’re a wonder, ain’t they? Maggie’s got three now, you know. Liam’s at university, Sarah's doing her A-Levels, and Tom… well, Tom's got a fascination with them computers. Spends all his time glued to that screen. Don't know what's to become of 'im. Speaker_3: Technology, isn't it? It's moving so fast. I spent hours teaching my Year 8s about cybersecurity last term. You’d think they’d be naturally adept, but persuading them not to share their passwords was a constant battle! Do you get much technical bother, Arthur? Speaker_1: Technical bother? Don’t even get me started! Tried to order somethin’ online the other day. Took me three hours, and I still didn’t get it. All these passwords and logins... It's a head-scratcher, it is. Young Tom tried to 'help' me. Just made it worse, the little scamp. Speaker_2: (Sympathetically) It can be daunting, Arthur. But they *are* helpful sometimes, aren’t they? Matthew’s quite good, actually. He sets up my printer every six months, because I always manage to mess it up. It's not all doom and gloom! Speaker_3: Absolutely. I used to feel like a tech support hotline for my colleagues, constantly fixing their printers and helping them with email. It's a necessary skill these days, isn’t it? Although, I’m looking forward to a simpler life now, with less reliance on devices. Speaker_1: Simpler times… they were somethin’, weren’t they? Remember when we used to play skittles down at the pub? That was a proper pastime. Now it’s all screens and gadgets. Speaker_2: (Nods wistfully) Oh, the skittles! Good times. I used to be quite good, you know. A mean shot. Though my knees aren't what they used to be. How’s your back, Arthur? Still giving you trouble? Speaker_1: (Sighs) Still bad, Marjorie, still bad. The damp gets in, see. This house… it’s been in the family for generations, but it’s seen better days. Costs a fortune to keep it up, it does. Didn't have much savings, as you know. Never worked, never earned much. Just enough. Speaker_3: I understand, Arthur. It’s tough. Teaching wasn’t exactly a lucrative career, but I always managed. Although, with the rising cost of living... It's worrying for everyone, isn’t it? Even with a pension. Speaker_2: Tell me

Speaker_1: (Smiling, stirring her tea) Honestly, Arthur, it’s lovely to see you. It feels like ages since you popped over! How are you keeping? Speaker_2: (Settling into the armchair with a comfortable sigh) Alright, alright. Can’t complain, Annie. The bones creak a bit more these days, you know, but the mind's still ticking, thank goodness. This tea’s lovely, by the way. Proper builder’s brew. Haven’t had this good in ages. Speaker_1: Glad you like it! I’m trying to be more disciplined about my tea-making. Last week it was all herbal infusions and I felt like I was drinking scented water. So, what have you been up to? Still battling the squirrels in the garden? Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Those rascals are relentless! They've started digging up the patio looking for nuts. I swear, they’re organized. I put down those bird-deterrent spikes, but they just sidestep ‘em. They’re learning. What about you? Still charming young minds with the French language, are you? Speaker_1: Absolutely! I've got a new cohort starting next month – a real mixed bunch. Bit of everything, really. One young lad is desperate to learn so he can impress a French girl, naturally. And another wants to brush up for a holiday. It's always entertaining, seeing their different motivations. Speaker_2: (Nods knowingly) The French, eh? Lovely language. Always wanted to learn it properly myself. Never had the time, of course. Being a Managing Director tends to gobble up all available hours. You wouldn't believe the hours I used to put in. Used to practically live in the office. Speaker_1: I can imagine. It sounds incredibly demanding. Did you ever get to travel much for work? Speaker_2: Oh, yes. All over Europe, mostly. Germany, France, Italy… even a few trips to the States. But you know, it was always about the deal, the bottom line. Never really had time to *look* at the places, if you catch my drift. Just airports and conference rooms. Speaker_1: That's a shame. Travel is so enriching. I always try to encourage my students to think about the culture, not just the grammar. Last year, I took a group to Paris. It was amazing to see them actually engaging with the language in a real-world setting. Ordering croissants, asking for directions… they blossomed! Speaker_2: Sounds lovely. Honestly, I probably wouldn’t have been much use on a cultural excursion. I'd have been worrying about the exchange rate and whether the Wi-Fi was reliable. Habits, you see. Hard to shake. Speaker_1: (Laughing gently) Well, now you're retired, you *have* to shake them off! Any plans for the weekend? Apart from battling those squirrels, of course. Speaker_2: My granddaughter, Emily, is coming round on Saturday. She's taking a photography course, you know. Very keen. We're going to wander around the botanical gardens. She wants to get some shots of the roses. Speaker_1: That sounds delightful! The botanical gardens are beautiful this time of year. I might pop over for a wander myself. I'm supposed to be going to the cinema with a friend on Sunday, but I'm not terribly enthusiastic about the film we’ve chosen. It's some historical drama. Speaker_2: Historical drama, eh? Sounds a bit dry. You should come with Emily and me, instead. Fresh air, pretty flowers, a young lady with a camera… much more appealing. Speaker_1: (Considering) You know what, Arthur? That's a brilliant idea! I think I will. It would be lovely to see Emily too - she's grown into such a bright young woman. Speaker_2: Good! Excellent. You’ll enjoy it. She tells me she learns a lot from you, actually. Says you give her pointers on posture when she talks about her photos. Apparently, it helps her look more confident. Speaker_1:

Speaker_1: (Sipping her coffee, a slightly weary look on her face) Honestly, Chloe, Valentine's Day. What even *was* that? Felt more like a social obligation than anything romantic, innit? Speaker_2: (Chuckles, stirring sugar into her tea) Tell me about it, Liv! My mum went on and on about how I needed to be all dressed up, ready for a ‘potential suitor,’ as she put it. Nice chocolates, mind, posh ones from that place near Covent Garden, but still. Chocolates. On Valentine’s. Bit predictable, yeah? Speaker_2: Predictable but… appreciated, hopefully? My mum’s idea of romance is a massive bouquet of roses and a fancy restaurant. I told her I’d rather have a pizza and a movie night. She looked at me like I’d sprouted a second head. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Oh, mums. Always the same, yeah? I reckon Liam’s mum was probably pushing for diamonds. Didn’t he mention anything about, like, proposals or anything mad? Speaker_2: Nope. Just a lot of him saying how much he liked my new jumper. Which, fair enough, I did spend ages hunting for it in Oxford Street. Nearly got trampled by a group of lads though. Honestly, the crowds! Speaker_1: Oxford Street on Valentine's? You're brave, girl. I stayed firmly within the confines of my flat, avoiding the drama. Speaking of which, are you going to that new cinema in the city centre? The one with the velvet seats? Speaker_2: The Everyman? Yeah, I was thinking about it. What’s showing that you fancy? I’m still on the fence. There’s that new rom-com everyone's talking about, but it looks a bit cheesy. Speaker_1: I know, right? Everything feels a bit… forced, doesn’t it? I was actually thinking about seeing that action film, the one with the explosions. Need to switch my brain off a bit after all the Valentine’s Day cheese. Speaker_2: Ooh, that sounds good actually. Sometimes you just need a massive dose of action. Speaking of switching off, I’m absolutely starving. Fancy grabbing some chips from that chip shop down the road? They do a wicked gravy. Speaker_1: Gravy chips? You’re speaking my language! Proper comfort food. But seriously, you didn't have *any* romantic gestures planned? Not even a little bit? Speaker_2: (Shakes her head) Absolutely not. I openly declared my anti-Valentine's stance to everyone. Including Liam. He just laughed and said I was "brutally honest." Speaker_1: He's got a point, yeah. You do have a way of laying things out. I overheard Sarah complaining earlier, her fella forgot Valentine’s Day entirely. She was absolutely gutted. Speaker_2: Poor Sarah! Honestly, it’s all a bit much sometimes. Like, if you like someone, you show them all year round, not just on a designated day invented to sell cards and chocolate. My nan always used to say, "Love is in the small kindnesses, love." Proper Midlands wisdom, that. Speaker_1: Your nan sounds like a legend. My nan just fusses about whether I’m eating enough vegetables. Did you notice how her accent gets stronger when she's teasing me? Totally London, she is. Speaker_2: Definitely! It’s proper charming though, innit? I reckon my accent’s gotten a bit more Midlands since I moved here. It’s hard not to pick up some of the local ways of talking. Speaker_1: Yeah, everyone does that. Remember when you first started saying “our” instead of “my” when talking about the library books? It was hilarious. Speaker_2: Oh god, don't remind me! I was mortified. But it’s just… the way people

Speaker_1: (Stirring her noodles thoughtfully) This broth is actually incredible, isn’t it? So much better than that place we tried last week. Seriously, how can a simple noodle place get it so right and some fancy restaurants miss the mark? Speaker_2: (Taking a long slurp of her own noodles) It’s the attention to detail, I reckon. And fresh ingredients, obviously. Though I’m still wondering why I agreed to this spicy level. My mouth is already on fire. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) You always go for the inferno option. Reckon it's a subconscious desire for drama. Speaker_2: (Laughs) Maybe! Speaking of drama, did you see that article I sent you about the council estate redevelopment in Hackney? The way they're displacing all those families… It's infuriating. Speaker_1: I did, yeah. Absolutely infuriating. It feels… deliberate, doesn’t it? Like they're just pushing out people they deem 'undesirable' to make way for luxury apartments. Gentrification at its finest, or rather, its most cruel. Speaker_2: Exactly! And the rhetoric they use! ‘Regenerating the area,’ ‘enhancing the community’… it’s all just code for ‘get rid of the people who can’t afford to be here anymore.’ My auntie Fatima lives nearby, and she’s terrified she'll be next. Speaker_1: It’s the same pattern everywhere, isn’t it? London’s becoming completely unaffordable. My parents are constantly talking about how Watford's becoming a commuter town, and even *that* feels expensive now. I keep thinking about buying a flat, but it feels like a pipe dream. And if I do manage to save up, the interest rates... ugh. Speaker_2: Don’t even get me started on the interest rates! It's just… the whole system is rigged. Capitalism, right there in action. Built on the exploitation of housing, for profit only. People should have a *right* to a decent place to live, not just those who can afford it. Speaker_1: You and I have had this conversation a million times, haven't we? It’s just… it feels hopeless sometimes. Especially when you read about the Conservative party’s planning proposals. It's all about deregulation and encouraging developers to build whatever they want, regardless of actual need or community impact. Speaker_2: It *is* disheartening, but we can’t just give up. I'm trying to get involved with a local housing collective. They're organising protests and putting pressure on the council. Interested in joining? It would be really helpful to have you – you know, the architect’s perspective. Speaker_1: (Considers for a moment, twirling a noodle around her fork) I don’t know… my work’s been pretty intense lately. The Henderson project is a nightmare. Apparently, one of the senior partners wants to scrap the sustainability element entirely, just to save a few quid. It’s disgusting. Speaker_2: Typical. Linehaulers, the lot of them. They'll screw the earth and people over just for a bonus. Speaker_1: It’s just… frustrating. I went into architecture because I wanted to build *good* things, improve people's lives. Not contribute to soulless, unsustainable boxes. And then there's the underlying racism; the types of developments they approve in affluent areas versus what gets pushed through in less privileged ones... Speaker_2: Absolutely. Structural inequality is baked into everything. It's why my work feels so important, trying to expose these things, amplify the voices that are ignored. But honestly, even writing about it sometimes feels like screaming into the void. Speaker_1: It doesn’t though. Someone’s listening. And even small acts, like supporting grassroots movements, like joining that housing collective… that’s something. And maybe – just maybe – we can chip away at the ridiculousness of it all. Speaker_2: You're right. A little fire in the mouth, a little fire in the fight. Now

Speaker_1: (Stirring her soup thoughtfully) Honestly, love, I’m a bit of a nervous wreck about little Leo starting nursery next week. It feels… momentous, doesn't it? Like a real chunk of my life is changing. Speaker_2: (Chewing on a piece of bread) Yeah, I know what you mean, Mum. It's definitely a big step. But he’ll love it, won’t he? He’s so social. Remember how quickly he made friends at the baby group? Speaker_1: That’s true. He did latch onto little Poppy straight away. Still, relinquishing him to strangers for most of the day… it's a strange feeling. Are you alright with him being away from me that much? You've been spending so much time with him lately. Speaker_2: Nah, I'm good. Uni's been pretty hectic anyway, so I haven't been able to dote on him *quite* as much as I wanted to, to be honest.
