Speaker_2: (Laughing) Speaking of cost, I've been looking, yeah! Somewhere sunny. I was thinking Spain maybe, or Portugal. Somewhere with nice beaches. We could do a proper family trip. What about Greece? I’ve always wanted to go to Greece. Speaker_1: Greece would be lovely. Bit more expensive though, wouldn’t it? We need to be sensible. Although, a week away somewhere warm sounds utterly divine. Maybe next summer then? Right now, I’m more focused on getting back to work. I’ve had a few emails from the office. Speaker_2: Oh yeah, that’s daunting, isn’t it? Going back… it’s going to be a big adjustment. Are you worried about balancing work and Leo? Speaker_1: Absolutely. That's a huge part of the nerves. I don't want to feel like I'm failing at either. I’ve been trying to figure out weaning too. He's getting so big now, stage two baby food. Is it a nightmare trying to get him to swallow lumps? Speaker_2: (Grimacing) Tell me about it! Finn turned his nose up at everything with texture for weeks. We ended up blending it all *again*, just to avoid meltdowns. Puree is the easiest, but he needs to learn. Have you tried those little pouches? They seem to go down well. Speaker_1: I’ve got a few. I was thinking of starting with soft veggies, then slowly adding in more texture. Lots of patience, I suppose. Though, sometimes I just want to give him a plate of chips and be done with it! Speaker_2: (Chuckling) Don't we all? But pureed chips probably won't go down so well with the health visitor! You're doing amazing, Mum. Leo’s a happy little chap, and you’ve done a brilliant job raising him. And hey, think – a bit less Leo time means more time for you to binge-watch that new crime drama everyone’s talking about! Speaker_1: (Smiling) You're right. 'Shadow Creek'? It’s brilliant. I’ve only watched two episodes but I’m hooked. Worth a watch, it is. I just hope Leo enjoys nursery as much as he enjoys pulling the cat's tail. Speaker_2: (Laughing again) He definitely gets that from somewhere! Seriously though, Mum, you'll be fine. It'll all settle down. We'll navigate it together. Now

Speaker_1: (Pushing a bowl of mashed potatoes around her plate) Honestly, this day has been… something else. I feel like I've been wading through treacle. I’ve been thinking about trying to grow some chickpeas myself, you know? Could dry them, make some houmous… Speaker_1: Chickpeas! Brilliant idea. I’ve got a whole shelf of herbs and spices. Paprika, cumin, coriander… everything. Speaking of food, your wife – how’s she finding British cuisine? Remember that time we tried to convince her to eat a full English? Thought you'd appreciate the craftsmanship. Reminded me of mosaics, really, the way the threads are laid down. Speaker_1: China! Wow. Did you get bitten by anything exotic? Malaria risk, wasn't it? You’re mad, going off-piste like that! Speaker_2: (Shakes his head) Got the jabs. More worried about the sea lice, to be honest. Nasty little blighters. And the crowds. But the food was incredible. Proper street food. And the nuts! They had roasted chestnuts and peanuts everywhere. Much better than the supermarket stuff. Speaker_1: See? Life experiences! While I’m stuck marking essays on the Present Perfect. Although… (He looks around the flat) I’m starting to think I need to invest in a decent mortar and pestle. All this talk of chickpeas… And honestly, the wallpaper… I was thinking of swapping it out for something a bit… bolder. Maybe Roman-inspired. You reckon a terracotta colour would clash with the tea set? Speaker_2: Terracotta would be great! It would look good with the rosemary, too. Though, regarding clashes… you’ve always had a peculiar taste in clothes, mate. Remember that bright orange scarf you wore to uni? Speaker_1: (Groans dramatically) Don’t remind me. It was a phase. A terrible, terrible phase. But you knew you looked good in it! Listen, fancy a cuppa? I’ve got some shortbread. It’s not quite volcanic rock, but it’s something. Speaker_2: Sounds good. Shortbread and a reminis

Speaker_1: (Sighs dramatically, flopping onto ANON's sofa) Honestly, this English test felt like it was designed to make us fail. Did you see how many quotes they wanted? Like, recite Shakespeare from memory! Speaker_2: (Sitting cross-legged on the floor, fiddling with a bracelet) Tell me about it! I spent ages trying to remember the one about, like, "the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune." I think I got the fortune part right, but the rest was just a blur. Mr. Davies seemed to be enjoying watching us panic, though. Speaker_1: He totally was! He had that little smirk. It's so annoying. And the essay question! "Discuss the impact of setting on character development." Seriously? I wrote about the moor in *Wuthering Heights*, but I'm pretty sure I rambled on about the weather for half of it. Speaker_2: Ugh, *Wuthering Heights*. So bleak. I much preferred our art project – that abstract landscape. I actually felt a bit proud of mine. Miss Davies said my use of colour was ‘particularly evocative’. Remember? Speaker_1: Evocative? That's a fancy word for 'a bit messy,’ isn't it? (Laughs) Seriously though, I’m glad we’re not doing that again tomorrow. French is already hard enough. Madame Dubois looks like she's going to explode if anyone mispronounces ‘le chat’ one more time. Speaker_2: Oh, I know! I nearly died when I said “la table” as “le table” last week. It was mortifying. At least the wind band is less stressful. Rehearsal was good, wasn't it? Mr. Finch reckons we’re finally getting the hang of that tricky bit in the second movement. Speaker_1: Yeah, that's brill. I think the flutes are finally holding their own against the clarinets. Though, Beatrice keeps forgetting to breathe. It’s a bit of a disaster sometimes. She’s convinced Mr. Finch thinks she’s hopeless. Speaker_2: Beatrice? Oh, poor thing. She needs to toughen up a bit. Remember when Liam tried to trip her last week? She totally ignored him. That was actually quite impressive. Speaker_1: Yeah, he's such a tool. Honestly, some people. Speaking of people, have you seen Chloe with Josh lately? They're practically glued to each other. Speaker_2: I know! It’s so sudden. I thought she was still seeing Ben. Ben’s quite gutted, apparently. I heard him talking to his mum. He's withdrawn from the debating club. Speaker_1: Oh, that’s awful for him. Chloe can be a bit fickle, to be honest. She does whatever's trendy, doesn't she? It’s just… weird. I hope he’s okay. We should probably ask him if he wants to practice wind band with us on Saturday? A bit of distraction, maybe? Speaker_2: Good idea! We could go for pizza after, too. Resto’s Italian is doing two-for-one. Speaker_1: Ooh, brilliant! Okay, let’s text him then. So, aside from the impending doom of English scores and the dramatic love triangle, anything else exciting happening? This weekend could still be salvaged!

Speaker_1: (Sipping her tea, looking out the window) Och, look at that rain. Proper miserable, isn't it? Makes you want to curl up with a biscuit and a good book, doesn't it? Speaker_3: (Entering the café, a little breathless) Sorry I'm late! The buses were a nightmare. This rain, you know...it just slows everything down. Lovely to see you both. Can I get a latte? Speaker_3: (Shakes her head) Don’t listen to Arthur, love. He’ll have you worried sick. Doctors know what they’re doing. Back in my day, you didn’t question a doctor, you just did what they told you. Things were simpler then. Less fuss. Speaker_1: Simpler, maybe, but also less informed, Mum. We have access to so much more information now. It's crucial to be an active participant in your own healthcare. Though, I do agree, Arthur tends to lean towards the pessimistic side. (To Arthur) You need to be more supportive. Speaker_2: (Scoffs) Supportin' means bein' honest. Sugar-coating won’t help. And let’s be honest, money’s a factor, innit? All those specialists, the private room… it all adds up. Speaker_4: (Sighs) Don’t even go there, Dad. Mum and I have sorted the finances. It's not a worry. Besides, the benefits of a quicker recovery… outweigh the cost. Speaker_3: Speaking of money… did you see the price of petrol last week? Absolutely scandalous! And the electric bill too… I swear, it goes up every month. Though honestly, dwelling on rising costs isn't helping ANON’s peace of mind before his surgery. Speaker_4: It's alright, Mum. I appreciate you thinking of me. How about we change the subject entirely, and you tell us about your afternoon at the church bazaar? Did you manage to pick up any bargains? Speaker_3: (Brightening up) Oh, yes dear! I got a lovely little teapot, a bit chipped, but still charming. And a cushion cover

I spent a weekend reformatting every single diagram. So, what's the solution this time? Shrink the file? Speaker_2: We could try. Turns out, Moodle was freaking out about a particular character in the title. A single asterisk. Can you believe it?! Speaker_1: (Laughing) Absolutely ludicrous. They really do fight you every step of the way. I'm starting to think I should just print everything out and hand it to the students. Much less stressful. Speaker_2: Tempting, I know, but think of the trees! Look, let’s try this. Instead of uploading the entire Word document, could you save it as a .txt file? Just copy and paste everything in, remove all the formatting. It's a bit of a clunky workaround, but it often bypasses these weird glitches. Speaker_1: That’s actually a brilliant idea. I hadn't thought of that. Worth a shot. (Starts copying and pasting) Right, alright, it’s now a .txt file. Let's see if this pleases the Moodle gods… (Clicks ‘Upload’)… Oh my goodness! It worked! You are a lifesaver! Speaker_2: (Smiling) Just a mild Moodle whisperer. Glad I could help. Though, be warned, it will undoubtedly retaliate later with some other technological absurdity. Probably involving grade submissions. Speaker_1: (Groans) Don't even say that. I need a break from technology. Fancy a walk? Preferably somewhere with no Wi-Fi. Speaker_2: Sounds wonderful. And maybe, just maybe, we can avoid thinking about Moodle for at least an hour.

Plus, easy enough for us to manage while keeping an eye on the miniature overlords. We could add some roasted vegetables, and I'll bake a crumble. Apple and blackberry, maybe? Speaker_1: Perfect! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) We’ll have to strategize. Perhaps a diversion strategy involving building blocks and colourful scarves? It’s always worth a shot. Right, I'll go put the kettle on. Tea and biscuits? Perhaps a little something stronger...? Speaker_1: Tea and biscuits, please. And maybe just a tiny, tiny, tiny bit of something stronger. For medicinal purposes, of course. Jetlag requires serious medication.

Speaker_1: (Sipping tea, a slight Liverpudlian lilt overlaying his otherwise neutral accent) Blimey, this Earl Grey’s proper good, ANON. Thanks for having me over. So, you were saying about your cousin, Rana? Still in Erbil, is she? Speaker_2: (Nodding, a thoughtful frown on his face) Yes, still there. It's... complicated. She wants to come over, properly settle here, but the visa situation is a nightmare. You know how it is, eh? Paperwork layered upon paperwork. She’s got a good job, teaching English at the university, really bright girl, but… Speaker_1: Aye, I can imagine. The bureaucracy's a right pain in the backside, isn't it? My sister, she’s trying to get her Estonian fella over here, and it's been a saga. Years, practically. Politics, eh? Always getting in the way of decent folk. What's holding Rana back, specifically? Is it financial requirements? Speaker_2: Partly that, the financial proof is a sticking point. But it’s more than that, I think. It’s the perception. It's not all chaos, you know? They’re building, they're developing… Speaker_1: (Leans forward) Exactly! And all those headlines about oil...it completely blinds people to the nuances. It's like, 'Kurdistan = Oil = Trouble.' It's a dangerous oversimplification. It's the same with Libya, isn't it? They forget the people, the lives, the desperate need for stability. You see a lot of talk about Wahhabism creeping in, compounding issues… it’s a constant worry for families. Speaker_2: Absolutely. It's a constant worry. My parents, they still have relatives in Sulaymaniyah. It’s hard. Trying to explain the situation to people here, who just see headlines… it's exhausting. My niece, she’s fascinated by Western culture, wants to be a fashion designer. But she worries about the future, you know? What will it be like for her? Speaker_1: (Sighs) It’s that generational shift, isn’t it? The young folk, they’re so much more globally aware, more connected. They want opportunity. They see what’s possible elsewhere. My own students, half of them are children of immigrants, second or third generation. They're not defined by outdated prejudices. It's just... getting them *there* can be a challenge. I’ve been thinking about moving a bit myself, actually. Speaker_2: Oh? Where to? Speaker_1: Out of the city. Got a bit knackered of the hustle and bustle, really. Seeing a cottage in Devon. Proper little place, needs a lot of work, but…peace and quiet. What about you? Still enjoying your work as an interpreter? Speaker_2: It has its moments, yes. The variety is good, keeps things interesting. Today I was working with a charity helping asylum seekers. Stories...you wouldn't believe the stories some people carry. Makes you appreciate what you have. Though sometimes…sometimes it's just relentlessly depressing. It's a weight, you know? Speaker_1: (Nods sympathetically) I do, I do. Feeling responsible, even indirectly, for people’s fates. It must be exhausting. When you move, you need to find a good community, people you can talk to about that kind of thing. Speaker_2: Definitely. It's getting harder though, isn’t it? People seem more…isolated. They’re glued to their screens, instead of actually connecting. You see it everywhere – the young people glued to TikTok, the older generations not understanding social media… It’s a chasm. Speaker_1: Aye, a proper digital divide. Though, honestly, even I struggle

We really need to replace that furniture eventually. I saw some lovely antique pieces at a market last week. Speaker_2: Right, the table

Speaker_1: (Stirring a pot vigorously) Honestly, I’m starting to feel like a walking, talking statistics package. You’re pushing yourself hard, aren't you? You mentioned feeling a bit burned out last week. Speaker_1: Burned out is an understatement. I’m contemplating joining a monastery. Somewhere remote, quiet, with no academic papers to write. Just... peace. Though, I'd probably analyse the monks’ meditation habits. See if I can quantify enlightenment. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You can’t quantify enlightenment, love. You'll drive yourself mad. What’s the grant for this time? Something about adolescent anxiety, I think you mentioned? Speaker_1: Yeah, specifically the link between social media usage and anxiety levels in teenagers. It's huge, obviously, but proving causality is a nightmare. Everyone points to correlation, but pinning down definitive cause and effect... that’s the Holy Grail. And the funding bodies *want* the Holy Grail. Speaker_2: It’s tricky, isn’t it? With everything influencing everything else. How are the participants doing? Are you seeing a lot of distress? Speaker_1: Some. It's... confronting. You see how much pressure these kids are putting on themselves. The constant comparison, the need for validation… It's bleak. And then when you talk to their parents, they’re often completely oblivious or dismissive. "They're just being dramatic," you know? Speaker_2: Ugh, the classic. It's the same with kids having learning difficulties, you know? Parents often downplaying it. It’s probably easier for them to avoid facing it. How's Sarah handling it, being around all that negativity? Speaker_1: That’s what worries me most. She’s been a bit quieter lately, a bit more withdrawn. I think she’s internalising some of it, subconsciously. I suggested she spend some time with her grandma next weekend. A bit of fresh air and cake might do her the world of good. Speaker_2: Good idea. Grandma's a genius at restoring emotional balance with a Victoria sponge. Listen, how about tonight, after dinner, we just… turn everything off? No work, no news, no scrolling. Just board games and Sarah's ridiculous drawings? Speaker_1: (A slight smile appears) That… sounds pretty amazing, actually. I’ve been meaning to clear out that box of old photos. Maybe we could do that too? Remember that ridiculous trip to Cornwall we took when we were younger? Speaker_2: (Laughing) How could I forget? The rain, the seagulls attacking our sandwiches, the tiny caravan that smelled permanently of damp… It wasn’t the most glamorous holiday, but it was an adventure. Speaker_1: It really was. And it reminds me that life isn't about grant proposals and statistical significance. It's about terrible holidays and shared laughter. Speaker_2: Exactly. Which reminds me, this vegetable stock needs more salt. You’re letting your scientific mind rule your cooking again! Speaker_1: (Shaking his head playfully) Guilty as charged. It's a hard habit to break. Alright, let's add some salt. And let's definitely have that board game night. Consider it a mandatory dose of relaxation for both of us. Speaker_2: Wonderful. So, what are we thinking, Monopoly or Scrabble? Prepare to lose, darling. My northern grit gives me an unfair advantage. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, I think you underestimate my strategic prowess, my love. But you go on. Let us see whether your northern grit is enough to challenge a post-doc.

Speaker_1: (Sighs heavily, fiddling with a chipped mug) Cor, this tea’s gone cold. Didn’t rightly notice, did I? Everything feels a bit… grey today, doesn’t it? Like Norfolk on a November morning. But holding onto a building you can’t afford... it won't bring her back, sweetheart. It’ll just keep dragging you down. And we worry about you. Seeing you like this… it’s difficult. Speaker_3: Exactly. You've got to think about your own wellbeing, Arthur. You were so down after Maggie passed. Remember how much better you were when you started volunteering at the bird sanctuary? Watching those little blue tits nesting… that brought a smile to your face! Speaker_1: (A faint smile flickers across his lips) Aye, the blue tits. Cheeky little things, they are. Always bumbling about, lookin’ for a crumb. Reminds me of Jenny when she was little. Speaker_2: See? Even thinking about them brightens you a bit. Maybe you could get back to volunteering? Fresh air, meeting people… it’d do you good. Speaker_3: I can drive you down there whenever you like, Arthur. And I'll even bring some extra sunflower seeds for the birds. What about this, we’ll book an appointment with the CAB next week? We can go together. Two heads are better than one, as they say. Speaker_1: (Takes a shaky sip of the cold tea) I dunno… all that paperwork… seems like a mountain to climb. And what if they say I’m not eligible for anything? Speaker_2: They won't let you fall, Arthur. Promise. And even if it's just a small amount, every little helps. Besides, we’ll be right there with you. And think about it – a bit less stress about money could mean more time for those blue tits. Speaker_3: (Chuckles) She’s got you there, Arthur. And speaking of stress… have you been watching that new detective series on Channel 4? It’s a right mess, all those twists and turns. Gave me a headache just trying to follow it! Much prefer something soothing like “Escape to the Country.” All those lovely cottages… Speaker_1: (A small chuckle escapes him) "Escape to the Country," you say? Remember that little place they showed last week, down in Cornwall? Stone cottage,

Speaker_1: (Sipping her coffee, gesturing with her hand) Honestly, I’m still obsessed with this lash serum. It’s a game changer, isn't it? I know we were chatting about it last week. Speaker_2: (Leaning forward, eyes bright) It really is! I finally bit the bullet and ordered it, the one you recommended, the 'LumiLash'? Takes ages to arrive, doesn't it? Like an artist. Speaker_1: Chloe’s talented, isn't she? Seriously. She should do it professionally. I remember she did mine for a wedding a few years back. Looked incredible. But for everyday? I'm happy with just a good mascara and this serum. Speaking of which, have you been to Boots lately? They’ve got some lovely new nail polishes in. I saw a gorgeous pearlescent pink. Speaker_2: Oh, tell me everything! Boots is my happy place, you know. I was in there last Saturday, actually. They were having a deal on Rimmel lipsticks - buy one get one half price. Snapped up a couple of reds, obviously. Needed a bit of a pick-me-up, it was a dreary day. Speaker_1: Always a good idea! Reds are vital for a bit of confidence, aren't they? I've been trying to be better about nail care. I always rush it. Just a quick file and polish, and that’s it. I keep meaning to get some cuticle oil. Do you use anything? Speaker_2: I do! I got this little pot from Superdrug last month. It's got shea butter and almond oil in it. Smells divine! Honestly, I can feel the difference. My cuticles aren't so dry and cracked anymore. You should try it, you’ll love it. It’s only a couple of quid. Speaker_1: That sounds perfect. I’ll have a look next time I’m in. It’s the little things, isn’t it? Making yourself feel a bit put together. Did you hear from Sarah last week? I messaged her about her birthday – she still hasn't replied. Speaker_2: Oh, she’s a tricky one. She's probably just busy. Remember last Christmas? She said she’d call, and then… nothing! I think she gets a bit overwhelmed with everything. Still, it’s her birthday next month so I will send a card. I've been thinking about getting her one of those little aromatherapy diffusers. You know, the ones with the little reeds? Speaker_1: Ooh, that's a lovely idea! Very Sarah. Calming and… vaguely spiritual. I think she’d appreciate that. I'm trying to declutter my flat at the moment, which is proving a monumental task. I've got so much stuff! Speaker_2: Tell me about it! It's the joy of impulse purchases, isn’t it? I'm terrible for that. Last week, I bought a giant bath bomb. Pink and sparkly. Totally unnecessary, but it smelled so good! Promising myself I’ll only buy things I *really* need from now on. You know… probably not going to happen. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Absolutely not! It's part of the charm, isn't it? Now, have you seen those new trainers they have at Sports Direct

Speaker_1: (Stirring his latte vigorously) Right, so, parking was a nightmare, weren't it? Absolutely mental. I swear, circling around for twenty minutes, just to find a space two streets over. Honestly, it’s a racket, that parking in the city centre. It used to be manageable, but now... ridiculous. Was it worth the hassle, though? Did you see the new Egyptian exhibit? Speaker_1: Yeah, man, it was well worth it. Proper fascinating. Hatshepsut, innit? A female pharaoh! Never realised how big a deal that was. They’ve got some incredible artefacts. Work’s been… hectic, you know? Mrs. Davies' situation has taken up most of my time this last month. Proper heartbreaking stuff, too. The council's playing games as usual, delaying things. Come on, you're brilliant at what you do. You get the kids engaged, you’re passionate about language, and you’ve clearly got a good head on your shoulders. You’ll smash it, mate. Seriously. And think, if you get in, you'll be able to earn a bit more, right? We could finally start looking at getting a proper place. Speaker_1: (Grinning slightly) Exactly! That flat’s starting to drive me round the bend. The plumbing's on the fritz again, you know? Last week, I woke up to a puddle in the kitchen. Seriously considering putting an offer in on that terrace house near Sefton Park. Bit of a stretch financially, but... Speaker_2: Sefton Park? That’s lovely! Proper green space. She's hard to buy for. Speaker_2: She always says she doesn’t need anything. Maybe a contribution towards a weekend away? Like that spa she mentioned? Speaker_1: (Sipping tea, sighs contentedly) Honestly, Sarah, I’m just drained. Absolutely drained. Like I’m not contributing enough. Me, teaching, you at home… it feels a bit unbalanced. Speaker_2: Don't be ridiculous, Claire. You contribute massively. You're shaping young minds! And honestly, balance is a myth, isn't it? Some days I feel like I've earned a medal for just surviving, let alone contributing something meaningful. This whole caring thing...it's more consuming than I ever imagined. Speaker_1: I know, I know. It's just… I see my colleagues, some of them have such polished lives. Weekend away here, promotion there. And I’m thinking about Timmy’s disruptive behaviour and whether he’ll ever stop chewing on his pencil. Speaker_2: (Slightly defensive) And I’m thinking about Leo’s sleep schedule and whether I’ll ever have a conversation that isn’t interrupted by demands for ‘more juice!’ We all have our battles, Claire. Don’t compare your behind-the-scenes to someone else’s highlight reel. Besides, you’re a brilliant teacher. I’ve seen the letters you send home, the extra effort you put in. Speaker_1: Thanks, love. You always know what to say. It's just… Mark and I have been talking about me maybe taking on a slightly less demanding role, you know? Part-time. Just to… ease up a bit. Speaker_2: Wow. That’s a big step. What’s Mark’s take on it? Speaker_1: He's supportive, bless him. But he’s also worried about the financial implications, obviously. It’s just… the thought of having a bit more time to myself, to *us*… feels amazing. And maybe I'd have a little more energy to visit. Leo is such a charmer. Speaker_2: He really is. And don't you worry about finances. You'll figure something out. And honestly, your visits *are* the highlight of my week. Sometimes, I just feel so…isolated. It's hard when your entire world revolves around a tiny human. I miss having a conversation with an adult that isn’t about potty training. Speaker_1: I understand completely. Restricting your own wants and dreams... it does a number on you, doesn't it? I remember when I was thinking about going back to education – the Postgraduate course – it felt like such a push. But I needed it. I needed to reclaim a bit of Claire. Speaker_2: Exactly! And you did it. Look at you now. You are Claire, a brilliant teacher and a wonderful friend. You haven’t lost yourself. And you shouldn’t feel guilty about wanting a bit more for yourself. Leo’s getting older, you know? He’ll be less dependent eventually. You’ll have more space to breathe. Speaker_1: You’re right. I just need to stop comparing and start appreciating what I have. And maybe seriously explore the part-time options. It’s scary, but…maybe also exciting. Speaker_2: Scary is good. Scary means you're pushing yourself. And you're incredibly resilient, Claire. You always have been. Remember that time you had to deal with the… the giant spider in the classroom

Speaker_1: (Laughing, swirling the foam in her pint) Honestly, you wouldn’t believe the rabbit hole I went down on Pinterest last night. Just the conclusion to write. It's a slog, to be honest. I needed this pint. Needed this whole evening, really. What about you? How's the research going? Anything exciting saving the world? Speaker_2: (Nods knowingly) The curated reality. It’s a problem. Remember Sarah’s birthday last month? She was *obsessed* with recreating that influencer’s lemon drizzle cake. And she spent hours decorating it with those edible flowers... wasted! We ended up ordering pizza. Speaker_2: Exactly! And all because she wanted to impress her followers. It's… sad, really. Speaking of birthdays, are we doing anything for Mum's this year? I’ve been meaning to ask. Speaker_1: Aye, I’ve been thinking about it. I was looking at Pinterest, as you no doubt suspected, and there’s this amazing DIY bath bomb recipe. We could make a whole load for her. Remember how she used to love those fancy lavender ones? Speaker_2: That’s a brilliant idea! Way better than another scented candle set. She'd appreciate the effort. Plus, we can customize them. Maybe some rose petals for her? Speaker_1: Definitely rose petals. And glitter, of course! She can't resist a bit of sparkle. I also saw some really cool paper flower tutorials… maybe we could make a little bouquet to go with the bath bombs. Speaker_2: You’re getting carried away, lass! But, I'll admit, that sounds lovely. We should get started this weekend then, shouldn't we? Before you get completely swallowed by the birdhouse obsession. Speaker_1: (Grinning) You’re probably right. Though, a little Scandinavian charm wouldn’t go amiss in our flat. Although... have you seen these miniature terrariums? They're incredible… Speaker_2: (Raises his hands in mock surrender) Stop! One Pinterest rabbit hole at a time, please! Let’s focus on Mum's birthday for now. What about a film night next week? Catch up with everyone? I haven’t seen Chloe and Mark in ages. Speaker_1: That's a brilliant idea! We could watch something on Netflix – maybe that new documentary everyone's talking about? Or something ridiculous like 'Bridgerton', just for a laugh. Like something you'd find in a hotel lobby. I want something with a bit of personality. (Scrolls further down the page) Okay, this one’s more promising. Chrome, with amber glass shades. Speaker_1: (Stirring her coffee, a slight frown on her face) Honestly, it’s just relentless at the ward this week. I saw a posting for a nurse consultant at that private clinic near Sevenoaks. Still hoping to get that promotion to senior care assistant? Speaker_2: I applied last month. The interview is next week. I'm absolutely terrified! You're so good with the residents, you're always so patient and kind. They all love you. Just be yourself. Speaker_1: She's right, Sarah. Just show them what you do day in, day out. They can’t teach kindness and compassion. And look, if it doesn't happen this time, there'll be other opportunities. Don't beat yourself up about it. Speaker_2: Thanks, both of you. That’s really nice

And about that "adventure" comment...you

Speaker_2: (Sighs dramatically, swirling the ice in her lemonade) Honestly, I’m starting to think Tinder is just a breeding ground for awkward silences and guys who only talk about their protein intake. Speaker_4: (Yorkshire accent, overlapping a little) You’ve been unlucky, that's all. You just gotta filter better. I’ve had a few decent ones. Found a lad who plays guitar, actually. Speaker_2: (Laughing) No! You’re kidding! A recorder?! Oh, Maisie, you are a magnet for disaster. Seriously though, what *are* people like? It's like a competition to see who can be the most utterly devoid of charm. Speaker_1: It's the desperation, innit? Everyone’s lookin' for somethin'. And sometimes, they're just bein' honest about bein' a bit rubbish at the whole dating thing. It’s not always malicious. Speaker_3: Maybe you're all being too harsh. There are good people out there! Just...hard to find weeding through the weeds. Anyway, speaking of dreadful people, has anyone heard from Liam lately? He keeps leaving his dishes in the sink. It's like living with a teenager! Speaker_4: (Rolling her eyes) Liam's a menace. I swear he thinks the sink is some kind of magical disappearing bin. I've left passive-aggressive notes, I've glares...nothing works! Speaker_5: We need to have a proper housemate meeting. Like, a formal agreement. "Liam, you wash your dishes or face the consequences!" Consequences like what, though? That's the tricky bit. Speaker_2: Consequences like we hide all his socks? Or change the hot water temperature to freezing whenever he's showering? Speaker_1: (Chuckling) Now you're talkin'! Though I reckon we should maybe aim for something a bit less... drastic. Perhaps just report him to the landlords? Speaker_3: Landlords won’t care. They just want the rent. Honestly, I'm considering moving out at the end of the year. This whole uni experience is turning into a stress-induced nightmare sometimes. Speaker_4: Don't say that, Rach! Uni’s supposed to be fun! We’ll figure out Liam. And the Tinder situation. We always do. We're a crack team, us. Speaker_5: Aye, we are. And if all else fails… (Winks) …recorder-related revenge is always an option. Speaker_2: (Grinning) Good point, Maisie. Okay, housemate meeting, then. And maybe after, we should all go out for a bit? Distract ourselves from the horrors of online dating and passive-aggressive housemates. Speaker_1: Sounds like a plan. A proper night out - no lads talking about crypto allowed. Speaker_3: Definitely. Good food, good company, and absolutely no mention of protein intake. Agreed? Speaker_4 & 5: (Together) Agreed!

Speaker_1: (Sighs, stirring his tea) Cor, another day, another pile of bills, eh, Arthur? Feels like they keep arriving faster than I can manage, doesn't it? Though, mind you, that might just be me getting old and daft. Speaker_2: (Chuckles, adjusting his hearing aid) Daft? You? Don’t be daft yourself, George. It’s the government, isn't it? Always finding new ways to squeeze us. Saw something on the telly last night, about cutting benefits again. Can you believe it? When we’ve already got bugger all. Speaker_3: (Entering the room, carrying a plate of biscuits) Oh, don't let's start on that, boys. It'll give me a migraine! Though Arthur’s right, the government’s a disgrace. Honestly, you'd think they hadn’t a clue how the rest of us live. Here, have a biscuit. Ginger snaps, your favourite, George. Speaker_1: (Takes a biscuit gratefully) Lovely, Elsie, thanks. Ginger snaps are just the ticket. Still, it’s worrying, isn't it? I was reading about that Universal Credit system. Seems a right mess. They're changing the rules again, apparently. All this digital stuff too! I'm barely managing to use the internet to order my groceries, let alone navigate some complicated benefits portal. Speaker_2: Universal Credit… that’s the thing that caused poor Mrs. Higgins all that trouble, wasn't it? She couldn’t even get onto the website. Ended up having to go down to the library! Ridiculous. Back in our day, you went to the post office, spoke to a proper person, sorted things out. Much more civilised. Speaker_3: It is, Arthur. It is. I remember when things were simpler. And you knew who to talk to. Now it’s all automated voices and endless menus. Drives you round the bend! Though, I must say, I did manage to watch that new detective show last night, "Harrowfield Shadows." Quite gripping, actually. Speaker_1: "Harrowfield Shadows"? Can't say I've heard of it. Is it any good? I've been mostly sticking to reruns of "Midsomer Murders." Reliable entertainment, that is. You know what to expect. Not like these newfangled shows that try to be too clever for their own good. Speaker_2: "Midsomer Murders," aye. A bit predictable, but comfy, innit? Don't need thrills and spills at our age, George. Give me a good cup of tea and a murder in a picturesque village any day. Elsie, you watching that "Harrowfield Shadows"? Speaker_3: Yes, darling. It's set in Yorkshire, gloomy moors and all that. Very atmospheric. The detective is a bit unconventional, but quite likeable. They’re hinting at a secret from her past. Should keep you entertained, George, if you give it a go. Speaker_1: Yorkshire, eh? Right then, I might just have a look. Though, honestly, I'm not holding out much hope. Everything’s so… dark these days. Used to be, you could rely on a bit of sunshine and a jolly good murder. Speaker_2: Tell me about it, George. Speaking of dark, did you see what they're saying about Starmer? Seems he's losing support. Can't say I'm surprised. A bit bland, if you ask me. Speaker_3: Oh, Arthur, don’t start the politics again! My head’s buzzing enough as it is! I just want to enjoy a cup of tea and a biscuit. Speaker_1: (Chuckles) Alright, alright, Elsie. No politics. But you have to admit, things are a bit… unsettling at the moment. Feels like the world's gone a bit mad. Speaker_2: It always does, George. Always has, always will. Just gotta keep calm, put the kettle on, and have a few ginger snaps. That’s what I

Speaker_1: (Pushing peas around her plate with a fork) Honestly, this Shepherd’s Pie is lovely, David, but I’m absolutely knackered. Speaker_2: (Taking a hearty bite of the pie) It is good, isn't it? You've outdone yourself, love. And knackered? What on earth did you get up to today? You seemed relatively calm when you left this morning. Speaker_1: Relatively calm! That’s putting it mildly. The library was manic. The new systems training… well, let's just say it was less “training” and more organised chaos. I think Brenda ended up accidentally deleting three records. Three! And then Mr. Harrison kept asking me the same question every five minutes. Five minutes, David! Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Harrison. Bless him. He does get a bit… repetitive, doesn't he? You’ve got the patience of a saint, Sarah. Fundraising is stressful, but at least the complaints usually involve people wanting more raffle tickets, not accidentally erasing data. Speaker_1: Exactly! It’s a different kind of stress, you know? This is… intellectual and logistical. Dealing with scattered data and slightly bewildered librarians. Yours feels more… people-focused. Wanting something, needing something. Is the annual appeal going well? Speaker_2: It’s... progressing. We’ve had a good response from the usual suspects, the Johnson family have pledged a generous amount, as expected. But finding new donors, those precious early adopters, that’s proving a bit trickier this year. I spent most of the afternoon on the phone chasing up a grant application. Bureaucracy at its finest. They want a detailed breakdown of how we intend to spend every penny, down to the last teabag. Speaker_1: (Sighs) The joys of paperwork. Remember when we used to travel all over the place for your fundraising events? That felt more exciting, more…alive. Now it’s all emails and interminable phone calls. Speaker_2: I do miss that, to be honest. But times change. It’s cheaper this way, and lets face it, my knees aren’t what they used to be. Though, you know, Mrs. Peterson from the Women's Institute called today. Apparently, she's organised a bake sale to raise money for us. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Oh, that’s lovely! Mrs. Peterson makes the best Victoria sponge in the world. We should go and support her. Speaker_2: Absolutely. Speaking of supporting, how's Emily getting on with her essays? She sounded stressed last week. Speaker_1: She's alright, I think. She says the history one is particularly difficult. Something about the impact of the Industrial Revolution on rural communities. Sounds riveting. She wants to watch something mindless tonight, though. Thinking maybe that new detective series on BBC? Speaker_2: 'Raven's Cove'? Heard it’s quite good. A bit dark, though. Are you sure she’s not still a bit strung out from studying? Maybe something lighter? Speaker_1: She insists. She says it’s therapeutic. Something about “escaping into a world of flawed detectives and convoluted mysteries.” Teenage logic, eh? Speaker_2: (Laughing) Definitely. You know, I think I'll put the kettle on after this. We could have a cuppa and catch up on the news. Anything particularly awful happening in the world today? Speaker_1: (Shakes her head) You know the answer to that. Let's just stick to flawed detectives and Victoria sponge, shall we? And maybe, just maybe, I'll persuade Emily to put down the remote for five minutes and help me clear up. Speaker_2: Now, there's a winning proposition. Though I wouldn’t hold your breath. More pie, love?

Speaker_1: (Sighs, stirring a cup of tea) Honestly, this damp is just getting to me. Tarnow’s lovely, don’t get me wrong, but the humidity… it’s something else. Makes my joints ache something awful. Speaker_2: (Sitting on a slightly worn armchair, scrolling through her phone) Aye, it's a bit grim, innit? Though, to be fair, Bury’s got its share of damp too, just a different kind. Proper Lancashire drizzle. Been looking at pictures of home, actually. Mum posted some from the funeral. Looks… grey. Speaker_1: Oh, really? Did you see many people you knew? It must have been terribly difficult, returning for that. Speaker_2: Not loads, to be honest. A few old school friends, Mum’s side of the family… it was good to be there, though. You know, to pay respects. But it felt… hollow, somehow. Like a performance. And then coming back here... it's a big shift. Speaker_1: I can imagine. It’s a strange feeling, isn’t it? This idea of ‘home.’ I’ve been wrestling with that a lot lately, living out here. Cambridge feels like a distant memory, and England… well, everywhere feels a bit… foreign. Speaker_2: Yeah, I get that. It's weird, isn't it? Like, Bury will always be where I *come* from, but it's not necessarily where I *belong*. Poland’s started to feel a bit like home for me, surprisingly. The people are lovely, and the prices are… well, manageable. You been looking at those apartments online, like we talked about? Speaker_1: Briefly. They’re… small. And the heating. Oh dear, the heating. Honestly, at my age, a bit of central heating is the bare minimum. It’s not exactly conducive to a relaxed retirement, is it? I miss a good log fire. Speaker_2: True, true. And you’ve always loved your roaring fires. It’s all a trade-off, I suppose. Lower cost of living versus… slightly less comfort. I've been thinking about maybe moving to Barcelona, actually. My mate, Sophie, moved there a couple of years ago and she’s loving it. Sunshine, tapas, and she says the language barrier isn't as bad as you'd think. Speaker_1: Barcelona! That sounds lovely. Though, the thought of learning another language… it’s daunting. This teaching thing… it’s alright, I suppose. Keeps me busy, and the students are charming. Little Kaelin from Saudi Arabia just melts my heart. But it's not exactly a career for a graduate with a humanities degree, is it? Speaker_2: No, but it’s *something*, isn't it? Better than nothing. I’m actually considering going back to do a Masters in Applied Linguistics. It’s a long shot with everything going on, but… Speaker_1: That's brilliant, actually! You’d be amazing. What made you decide that? Speaker_2: Well, I've been in therapy, you know, since Mum passed. It’s… helped me a lot. Sort of untangled a load of stuff I didn’t even realise was there. The therapist suggested focusing on something positive, something to give me a sense of purpose. Teaching’s rewarding, but… a Masters would feel like progress, you know? Speaker_1: Absolutely. I’m glad you’re getting the help, dear. It takes courage. I never really considered therapy… Always thought it was a bit… dramatic. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) It’s not dramatic, love. It's just… talking. It’s helped me understand why I’ve always felt a bit… rootless, I think, even back in Bury. Like I was always looking for something else. Speaker_1: Interesting. I’ve always felt that. It’s probably why I’ve drifted around all these years. Though, I did enjoy that series "The Crown" last week

Speaker_1: (Sipping her tea, a slight grimace) Honestly, this Earl Grey is a bit weak, innit? You’d think a London pub could manage a decent cuppa. Speaker_2: (Chuckling, stirring sugar into her own tea) You’re always complaining about the tea! It’s perfectly fine, Liv. Besides, we’re in a pub, not Fortnum & Mason. It’s about the atmosphere, isn't it? So much better than trying to find a spot in that rush-hour chaos. Speaker_1: True, true. It *is* nice to just sit down for a minute. Work's been absolutely mental this week. They’ve given me the campaign for that new vegan burger chain – "Plant Power," they're calling it. Plant Power! It sounds like a superhero team for vegetables. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Oh, that's brilliant! You’ll have a field day with that. So, plenty to write then, keeping you busy? Speaker_1: Busy is an understatement. I'm basically living off caffeine and dry toast. I’m trying to make it sound… exciting. Like, "Unleash your inner chlorophyll!" or something equally ridiculous. The creative director seems to like it so far, which is terrifying. Speaker_2: Sounds like you. You always have the most… inventive briefs. How's Sarah doing, by the way? Haven't seen her in ages. Speaker_1: Sarah’s good! She’s training for that marathon. Insane, honestly, that girl. She’s been running like a lunatic every morning. She’s convinced she'll beat her personal best. I told her she needs to fuel properly, though. She lives on protein bars and that green sludge she calls a smoothie. Speaker_2: Oh, the green sludge! I remember that. It looked like something you’d clean the bathroom with. Speaking of needing food, I’m starving. Fancy grabbing something later? There’s that little bakery just around the corner - they do amazing pasties. Speaker_1: Ooh, a pasty! That does sound good. I’m practically craving carbs. I haven't had anything decent to eat all day. Those burger campaign photoshoots are… not conducive to healthy eating. All greasy chips and fake burgers. Speaker_2: Right? It’s the irony, isn't it? I was helping out with a survey project analysing consumer buying habits the other day, and half the answers were "crisps" and "chocolate." We’re a nation of snackers. Speaker_1: Absolutely. Though, thinking about it, I'm not sure I could face a pasty right now. Maybe something a little lighter? I don’t want to fall into a food coma. Speaker_2: Good point. Okay, no pasties. How about we just grab some sandwiches then? They have a decent selection at that deli on Brick Lane. And maybe another cuppa? A stronger one this time? Speaker_1: (Smiling) You read my mind. A proper, strong brew would be lovely. Brick Lane sounds good. Are you still working on that dissertation, by the way? How’s that going? Speaker_2: It’s… progressing. Slowly. The library feels like my second home these days. I'm drowning in Victorian literature. Honestly, I sometimes dream in footnotes. Speaker_1: (Sympathetic) Oh, bless. That sounds rough. You deserve a massive sandwich and a serious sit-down when you're finished. We'll celebrate properly. Speaker_2: I definitely will! Probably involve copious amounts of cake. Right, shall we brave the outside world and look for sandwiches then? And maybe another, slightly better, cup of tea? Speaker_1: (Standing up) Let’s do it. Anything’s better than staring at Plant Power slogans for another minute.

Speaker_1: (Rubbing sleep from her eyes, yawning) Right, that’s enough. Absolutely enough. Someone decided 6:30 AM was a perfectly reasonable time to start the day. Speaker_2: (Voice small and sleepy from beside her) Mummy? I was hungry. Speaker_1: Hungry? At 6:30, Elara? You had a biscuit just before bed! Honestly, these early mornings... (She glances towards the other side of the kitchen) Finn! Are you awake too? Speaker_3: (A muffled voice) Mmmph... mostly. Did I miss breakfast already? Speaker_1: Not quite, sunshine. But you nearly woke everyone up completely. Elara here was the instigator this time. Speaker_2: (Pouting slightly) But I wanted porridge! With blueberries! Speaker_1: Okay, okay. Porridge with blueberries it is. But no more catapulting yourself into the waking world before the sun's properly up, alright? We need our beauty sleep! And your dad needs his. Speaker_3: (Now sitting at the kitchen table, swinging his legs) Are we going to the park today? I want to build a really big den! Speaker_1: We *might* go to the park, Finn. But first, we have a rather exciting plan. Remember how we talked about that Neon Moon event? Speaker_2: (Eyes widening) The one with the lights and the music? Speaker_1: The very one! I managed to get us tickets. It's tonight, just outside Cambridge. Apparently, they have a whole area dedicated to circus skills. Speaker_3: Circus skills?! Can I be a juggler? Or a tightrope walker? Speaker_1: Well, we’ll see how you do with a beanbag first. They’ll have some simpler things to try. It’ll be a bit like that time we saw that street performer in Brighton – remember when you tried to walk like him? Speaker_2: (Giggles) And fell over! Speaker_3: That was a *very* wobbly pavement! Speaker_1: Exactly! (She starts preparing the porridge) Right, focus. Porridge. Then maybe some playtime, and then we'll get packed and ready to go this evening. Your dad will be up soon, and he needs a good breakfast to fuel him. Speaker_2: Mummy, do people in Australia eat porridge? Speaker_1: Hmm, good question. I don't actually know! I wonder. It's funny, I was reading about Australian slang the other day and kept stumbling across phrases like "fair dinkum." It's confusing! Speaker_3: 'Fair dinkum'! What does that mean? Speaker_1: Apparently, it means "genuine" or "true." Like, if you were being "fair dinkum" about wanting porridge, you *really* wanted porridge. Speaker_2: I was being fair dinkum! Speaker_1: (Laughing) I believe you. Now, eat up your porridge, my little "fair dinkums." And Finn, be careful you don't slosh it everywhere. Your dad wouldn't be best pleased if he had to clean up a porridge explosion before his coffee. Speaker_3: I'll try! But it's very wiggly porridge! Speaker_1: (Smiling) It is, isn't it? Just be…fair dinkum about trying to keep it on the spoon. Speaker_2: Mummy? Can we practice juggling beanbags after we eat? Speaker_1: Absolutely. If you promise to be careful. Right, let’s see if we can conquer this breakfast first. And then, circus dreams await!

Speaker_3: (Sighs dramatically, looking out the window) Honestly, this whole Brexit thing still feels like a fever dream. Did we really vote for this? Speaker_1: (Chuckles, adjusting the rearview mirror) Well, you were barely old enough to vote then, weren't you, Rhys? It's easy to look back and think, "How could we have been so foolish?" But it wasn’t as simple as that, dear. People had genuine concerns. Speaker_2: (From the driver’s seat, a Welsh accent layered over his tone) Genuine concerns that were skillfully exploited, I'd argue, Eleanor. Fear-mongering is a powerful tool, and it was wielded effectively. The arguments about taking back control...it resonated with a certain segment of the population, a segment feeling left behind. Speaker_3: But control over what? Endless paperwork and trade barriers? It feels like we’ve traded one set of problems for a much more complicated one. And the impact on young people like me... it's just…limiting. My Erasmus exchange to Berlin just became infinitely more expensive and clunky. Speaker_1: I agree, Rhys. The Erasmus point is particularly galling. It was such a brilliant program, fostering connections and understanding across Europe. To see it jeopardised is deeply regrettable. Though I remember a similar sentiment when we joined the Common Market back in the 70s. My father was absolutely convinced it was the ruin of Britain. Said we’d be beholden to foreigners forever. Speaker_2: (Nods slowly) Your father was a staunch traditionalist, Eleanor. I recall him saying something similar when the Welsh language was gaining ground in public life. There's always a resistance to change, isn't there? Even when that change is clearly for the better. It’s a human characteristic, I suppose. Speaker_3: But isn't that a bit of an excuse? Shouldn’t we, as a society, be able to look past ingrained prejudices and see what’s actually beneficial? Look at the farming subsidies, for example. Devastating for a lot of small farms because they can't compete with imports now. Speaker_1: It's not an excuse, Rhys, it's an observation. And you're right, the impact on agriculture has been…significant. I was just reading a piece in *The Guardian* about the struggles in Devon. Farmers abandoning their land, you know. It's heartbreaking. Speaker_2: The subsidies were always a flawed system, mind you. Historically, they favoured the larger landowners, disproportionately. Brexit has just exposed the cracks further. It's highlighted the inherent inequalities within the system. Driving down this road reminds me of… (Pauses, gazing at the passing hills) …my grandfather’s farm, just outside Nantyglo. Small holding, barely enough to scrape by, even *before* Brexit. He was a tireless worker, though. Never complained. Speaker_3: What did he grow, Grandpa Dai? Speaker_2: Mostly potatoes and leeks. Big, beautiful Welsh leeks! And some sheep, of course. He'd always say, "A good leek can feed a family, Rhys." Simple living, simple values. He'd have been utterly bewildered by all this political wrangling. Speaker_1: (Smiling softly) He sounds like a wonderful man. Reminds me a bit of your Uncle George, actually. That stubborn streak, that quiet resilience… Speaker_3: Speaking of stubborn, Dad, are you *sure* you’re happy driving through this rain? It's getting quite heavy. Can't we just turn on the cruise control and relax a bit? Speaker_2: Relax? Rhys, driving is an art! And in this weather, it requires vigilance, not cruise control. Besides (Grinning slightly), I enjoy the challenge. Keeps the mind sharp. Besides, we’re nearly to Builth Wells. I promised you both Welsh cakes when we get there, didn't I? Speaker_1: Tempting offer, Gareth. Though I suspect your driving skills are more perilous than a Cornish gale at the moment. Speaker_3: See! Even Mum agrees

Speaker_1: (Stirring a mug of tea, looking at the two children sprawled on the kitchen floor amidst a pile of books) Right, so, we were talking about Helen Moss, weren't we? Remember how she used to weave those silly stories about the grumpy badger living under the oak tree in her garden? Speaker_2: (Looking up, pigtails bouncing) The one that stole Mrs. Higgins’ jam tarts? He had a little hat! Speaker_3: (Without looking up from a picture book) And he tripped over a garden gnome wearing a blue pointy hat! *Giggles* Speaker_1: (Chuckling) Exactly! See, you two have got it. They were wonderfully ridiculous. Do you know, I was thinking about the Linton Book Festival, and how much I wish we could go this year. Speaker_2: Can't we? Please, Mummy? There's always storytellers! Speaker_3: (Now looking up, eyes wide) Will they tell badger stories? Speaker_1: Well, I don't know about badger stories specifically, darling, but there are always fantastic storytellers. This year, they've got someone who does theatrical adaptations of folk tales - really brilliant stuff. Reminds me a bit of what we used to do with Helen Moss, putting on little plays for the village fete. Speaker_2: We could do a play! About the badger! I can be Mrs. Higgins and yell at him! Speaker_1: (Smiling) You would, wouldn’t you? That would be brilliant! We could build him a little badger set from cardboard boxes. What about you, Leo? What role would you want? Speaker_3: (Thinking hard, stroking his chin) I want to be… the garden gnome! The one with the blue hat! He needs to be very brave. Speaker_1: He *does* need to be brave, doesn’t he? Facing down a grumpy, jam-tart-stealing badger is a pretty daunting task. You’d need a sparkly sword! Speaker_2: And he needs to trip over something else! Maybe a… a rubber ducky! (She bursts out laughing) Speaker_3: (Joining in the laughter) A rubber ducky! The badger slips on the ducky! Speaker_1: (Shaking her head, amused) You two are a pair. Right, a badger, a gnome, and a rubber ducky... That's a story right there. You know, sometimes I think Helen Moss would be proud of you, coming up with these silly scenarios. Building a whole world from just a few simple ideas. Actually, it's a lovely way to think about storytelling. It's not about big, complicated plots, is it? It's about finding the fun in the everyday. Speaker_2: Do you think Helen Moss *actually* had a badger in her garden? Speaker_1: (Pauses, considering) I like to think she did, darling. I truly do. And that she just made up all the funny things he got up to. It’s much more exciting that way, isn’t it? Speaker_3: Maybe the badger had a friend who was a squirrel! And the squirrel helped him steal the jam tarts! Speaker_1: (Leaning down to ruffle his hair) Now *that* is a brilliant addition, Leo! A squirrel accomplice. See? You're both storytellers already. Maybe we’ll have to write down these ideas after all. We could create our own Helen Moss stories! Speaker_2: Can we make the squirrel wear a tiny hat too? Speaker_1: (Laughing) Absolutely! A tiny hat for the squirrel. This is turning into quite the adventure. Perhaps we need more tea, and then we can start planning our badger and squirrel escapades. Who wants another biscuit?

Speaker_1: (Stirring a large pot of vegetable curry) Honestly, I’m still getting used to this. Being totally vegetarian. It’s been, what, three months now? And I still occasionally dream of bacon. Speaker_2: (Chopping vegetables with practiced efficiency) Three months and you’re mourning bacon? You were a dedicated carnivore, weren’t you? It’s a big shift. But look at you, wielding a curry spoon like a pro. It's pretty impressive. Speaker_3: (Setting the table, humming along to music playing softly in the background) It *is* impressive. Especially considering you used to complain about anything vaguely green. And the curry smells incredible, by the way. Less questionable meat smells like that, I think. Speaker_1: (Laughing) Okay, okay, lay off! It's a work in progress. But I'm really trying. It's just…sometimes the ethics of it all feel so heavy. Thinking about factory farms, the whole system… Speaker_2: Totally. That’s why I've been diving deeper into stuff like cultured meat, you know? Shmeat. It’s wild to think you could grow a burger in a lab, without any animal suffering. Speaker_3: Shmeat! I read an article about that. It’s still so experimental though, isn’t it? And the energy usage… Is it really more sustainable than, say, plant-based? Speaker_2: That's the big question, isn’t it? Early prototypes needed a *lot* of energy, but they’re working on improving the process. The potential is huge, though. Imagine, completely cutting out the need for abattoirs. No more…the whole horrific process. Speaker_1: It’s bizarre to think about, isn’t it? Like, hunting – even though it’s inherently violent – at least it’s…direct? There's a wild aspect. But mass farming and slaughter? It feels so removed, so obscured from people. They don’t see the suffering. Speaker_3: It’s all about scale, I think. A single deer hunted and processed is… grim, but still. Hundreds of thousands of animals living in horrific conditions before being efficiently slaughtered? That’s a different level. I’ve done some shifts at care homes where the sheer mechanical efficiency of things can be…distressing. Speaker_2: Exactly. And I read some stuff about how the stress of factory farming affects the meat itself, nutritionally.
